Attempt 1
Question 1Incorrect

The database engineering team at Norwood Robotics, a biotechnology research lab that tracks sample metadata in Amazon DynamoDB, needs to return a list of items from a global secondary index on the Norwood-SampleRecords table.

Which DynamoDB API call can the team use in order to consume the LEAST number of read capacity units?

Scan operation using strongly consistent reads

Explanation

Incorrect. A Scan operation examines every item in the table or secondary index. This makes a Scan the least efficient access pattern regardless of consistency setting. Strongly consistent reads add even more RCU cost on top of that inefficiency, so this combination represents the worst-case scenario for RCU consumption. Keyword tip: "Scan" plus "strongly consistent" together signal the highest possible RCU cost among the listed options.
Query operation using strongly consistent reads

Explanation

Incorrect. A Query operation is more efficient than a Scan because a Query reads only matching items. However, strongly consistent reads consume twice the read capacity units of eventually consistent reads for the same item size, so this option is not the lowest-RCU choice. Keyword tip: strongly consistent reads always cost more RCUs than eventually consistent reads for the same amount of data.
Correct answer
Query operation using eventually consistent reads

Explanation

Correct. The Query operation retrieves items based on primary key or index key values. A Query reads only the matching items instead of scanning the entire table, so a Query is inherently more efficient than a Scan. For items up to 4 KB in size, one read capacity unit supports one strongly consistent read per second or two eventually consistent reads per second. Combining a Query with eventually consistent reads therefore consumes the fewest RCUs among all four options. Keyword tip: pairing "Query" (targeted access) with "eventually consistent" (half the RCU cost per read) signals the lowest-RCU answer.
Your answer is incorrect
Scan operation using eventually consistent reads

Explanation

Incorrect. A Scan operation reads every item in the table or index first, then filters out the results the team wants. This process consumes far more read capacity units than a targeted Query, because a Scan examines the entire dataset regardless of which consistency mode is used. Keyword tip: whenever a question mentions "Scan," expect higher RCU consumption compared to "Query."

This question tests understanding of how Amazon DynamoDB read capacity unit (RCU) consumption depends on two separate factors: the access pattern and the read consistency model. The access pattern is either Query or Scan. A Query reads only the items that match a specific partition key or sort key value, so a Query is always more efficient than a Scan, which reads every item in the table or index before filtering. The consistency model is either strongly consistent or eventually consistent. For items up to 4 KB, one RCU supports one strongly consistent read per second or two eventually consistent reads per second, so eventually consistent reads always cost half as many RCUs as strongly consistent reads for the same data. The lowest-RCU combination is therefore a Query using eventually consistent reads, and the highest-RCU combination is a Scan using strongly consistent reads.

Practical example: Norwood Robotics stores millions of sample records in a DynamoDB table and uses a global secondary index to look up records by experiment batch ID. Because the lab dashboard can tolerate results that are a few hundred milliseconds out of date, the database engineering team configures the dashboard to run a Query against the index using eventually consistent reads. This choice keeps RCU consumption low and reduces the provisioned capacity the lab needs to pay for, compared to scanning the entire table or requiring strongly consistent reads.

Question 2Incorrect

Keystone Dynamics, an automotive manufacturer, runs a fleet-management platform that stores vehicle telemetry and assembly-line sensor readings in a single Amazon DynamoDB table containing millions of records. This table handles a high volume of read and write requests from plants across several countries.

The engineering team now needs to add near-real-time processing on records as soon as they are inserted or modified in the table, without disrupting the existing write path.

What is the most efficient way to introduce this capability with MINIMUM modification to the existing application code?

Correct answer
Use AWS Lambda triggered by DynamoDB Streams to process the records

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level changes, including inserts, updates, and deletes, on the DynamoDB table. AWS Lambda can be configured as a trigger on the stream without any change to the application's existing write logic. This combination gives near-real-time, event-driven processing with low operational overhead. Keyword tip: when a question asks for reacting to DynamoDB item changes with minimal code changes, DynamoDB Streams paired with AWS Lambda is the standard serverless pattern.
Your answer is incorrect
Set up an Amazon Kinesis Data Stream to process updates from the DynamoDB table

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams can capture DynamoDB changes when Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB is enabled. However, this option requires building and managing separate consumer applications to process the data, which adds architectural complexity compared to a direct AWS Lambda trigger. Keyword tip: choose Kinesis Data Streams when multiple consumers, longer data retention, or high-throughput fan-out is needed; choose DynamoDB Streams with AWS Lambda when a single near-real-time processing trigger is enough.
Use Amazon SQS to queue incoming data and process it using Amazon EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS requires the application to explicitly send a message to the queue after each write. This means the existing write path must be changed, which violates the requirement for minimal code modification. Amazon SQS is also a pull-based queue, so the EC2 consumers must poll for messages, which adds latency instead of giving an event-driven, near-real-time response. Keyword tip: Amazon SQS needs producer code changes and consumer polling logic; it is not a native database change-capture mechanism.
Modify the application code to add processing logic after each DynamoDB write operation

Explanation

Incorrect. Adding processing logic directly inside the application after every write operation changes the existing write path. This directly contradicts the requirement for minimum code modification. This approach can also add latency to the write path and ties the processing logic to the write operation, which increases the risk of failure. Keyword tip: any option describing manual code changes on every write operation is a warning sign when the question asks for minimal application changes.

This question tests knowledge of event-driven architectures that react to changes in a DynamoDB table with minimal impact on existing code. DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes and integrates natively with AWS Lambda as an event source, so near-real-time processing can be added without touching the application's write path. Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB is a valid alternative, but it requires building and operating custom consumer applications, which adds complexity. SQS-based queuing and manual code additions both require direct changes to the application's write logic, so both violate the stated constraint. The decision logic centers on finding a native, serverless trigger mechanism that avoids modifying the producer application.

Real-world example: Keystone Dynamics could use DynamoDB Streams with AWS Lambda to detect abnormal sensor readings from its assembly-line equipment the moment a record is written, and trigger an automated maintenance alert. This keeps the existing telemetry-ingestion code untouched while adding near-real-time quality monitoring across all plants.

Question 3Correct

Automating the creation of Amazon ECS clusters with an Auto Scaling group requires a CloudFormation template that accepts the cluster name as a parameter. At Orchardvale Analytics, a cruise line operator that manages fleet-wide guest-services microservices on AWS, a development team builds such a template and first launches it with the input value 'OrchardvaleMainCluster', which deploys five EC2 instances across two Availability Zones.

The team then launches the same template a second time with the input value 'OrchardvaleSecondCluster'. However, the instances created during the second launch also register into 'OrchardvaleMainCluster' even though a different cluster name was specified.

What is the root cause of this issue?

The security groups on the EC2 instance are pointing to the wrong ECS cluster

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups control network traffic to and from EC2 instances. Security groups do not control which ECS cluster a container instance registers with. Keyword tip: security groups are a networking concept. Security groups are never involved in cluster membership or agent registration logic.
The EC2 instance is missing IAM permissions to join the other clusters

Explanation

Incorrect. The EC2 instances successfully register to a cluster. The cluster is just the wrong one, 'OrchardvaleMainCluster'. This proves that IAM permissions for cluster registration are working correctly. If IAM permissions were missing, the EC2 instances would fail to register to any cluster at all. Keyword tip: IAM permission problems cause complete registration failures or explicit AccessDenied errors. IAM permission problems do not cause registration to the wrong cluster.
The ECS agent Docker image must be re-built to connect to the other clusters

Explanation

Incorrect. The first launch of the CloudFormation template succeeded without any problem. This confirms that the ECS agent Docker image works correctly. The ECS agent Docker image does not need to be rebuilt. Keyword tip: if the same artifact works in one launch and misbehaves in another launch with different input, suspect the configuration or bootstrap logic. Do not suspect the artifact itself.
Your answer is correct
The cluster name parameter has not been updated in the /etc/ecs/ecs.config file during bootstrap

Explanation

Correct. The ECS container agent reads the ECS_CLUSTER value from the /etc/ecs/ecs.config file during EC2 instance bootstrap. The ECS_CLUSTER value tells the ECS container agent which cluster to join. If the CloudFormation template's user data script does not correctly insert the new cluster name parameter into this file for each launch, every new EC2 instance keeps registering to the previously configured cluster. In this scenario, that previously configured cluster is 'OrchardvaleMainCluster'. Keyword tip: when EC2 instances launched with a different cluster name parameter still join the original cluster, check how ECS_CLUSTER is set in the bootstrap script and in /etc/ecs/ecs.config.

This question tests understanding of how the Amazon ECS container agent determines cluster membership during EC2 instance bootstrap. The ECS container agent reads the ECS_CLUSTER value from /etc/ecs/ecs.config, which is normally set through user data in the launch template or launch configuration. When instances join an unexpected cluster, check whether the CloudFormation template's user data script correctly inserts the cluster name parameter into this configuration file for every new stack launch. IAM permissions, the ECS agent Docker image, and security groups do not control cluster registration, so none of them are valid root causes here. The correct troubleshooting approach is to trace the exact mechanism ECS uses for cluster assignment, which is bootstrap configuration, instead of investigating unrelated but plausible-sounding causes like networking or IAM.

Consider this scenario: Orchardvale Analytics runs a fleet-wide booking microservice on ECS and reuses one CloudFormation template to spin up a separate cluster for each ship class. If the bootstrap script hardcodes the cluster name instead of reading the CloudFormation parameter, every new ship-class cluster silently registers its instances into the original cluster, which can cause capacity and isolation problems across the fleet's reservation systems.

Question 4Incorrect

An initial deployment of an Amazon API Gateway API needs additional deployment stages—prod, test, and dev—associated with the existing deployment, with each stage routing to a corresponding AWS Lambda function variant that can be updated over time without requiring changes to the API Gateway configuration or the client-facing endpoint.

Northbridge Works, a social media analytics company headquartered in Austin, is implementing this configuration for its trending-topics API. Which of the following features must the developer add to achieve this? (Select TWO.)

Lambda X-Ray integration

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS X-Ray integration with Lambda enables distributed tracing and debugging of requests across services. X-Ray helps troubleshoot performance issues. X-Ray does not associate an API Gateway stage with a specific Lambda function variant. Keyword tip: X-Ray signals observability and tracing, not environment or version routing.
Your selection is incorrect
Mapping Templates

Explanation

Incorrect. Mapping templates transform request or response data between the client and the backend integration. Mapping templates can convert JSON to XML or override parameters. Mapping templates do not associate a stage with a specific backend Lambda function variant. Keyword tip: mapping templates signal payload or parameter transformation, not environment routing.
Correct selection
Stage Variables

Explanation

Correct. Stage variables are name-value pairs that a developer configures for each API Gateway deployment stage. Stage variables act like environment variables. Each stage, such as prod, test, or dev, can use a stage variable to reference a different backend value, such as a Lambda alias name. The API Gateway configuration does not change when the stage variable value changes. Keyword tip: stage variables let a stage point to different backend resources without changing the API definition.
Your selection is incorrect
Lambda Versions

Explanation

Incorrect. A Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of a function's code and configuration. Once published, a Lambda version cannot be updated. Because a Lambda version cannot be updated, a Lambda version cannot serve as a stable, evolving reference point for a stage like prod or dev. A Lambda alias, not a Lambda version, is the resource that a stage variable should reference. Keyword tip: versions are immutable, and aliases point to versions, so a changing stage should reference an alias.
Correct selection
Lambda Aliases

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda alias is a mutable pointer to a specific Lambda function version. A developer can update the alias to point to a new version over time. The alias ARN and alias name stay the same even when the underlying version changes. This stability lets dev, test, and prod stages reference a consistent alias while the function code evolves. Keyword tip: aliases provide a stable, updatable pointer to a Lambda version, which supports environment-based routing.

API Gateway stage variables and Lambda aliases work together to let a single API definition route to different backend resources depending on which stage is invoked. A stage variable holds a value, such as a Lambda alias name, that is unique to each stage (prod, test, or dev). The Lambda alias then acts as a mutable pointer to a specific Lambda version, so a developer can update the alias to a new version without changing the stage variable or the API Gateway configuration. Lambda versions are immutable and are the target that aliases point to, not something a stage should reference directly; mapping templates handle payload transformation, and X-Ray handles tracing, so neither feature supports this environment-routing requirement.

Use case: Northbridge Works, a social media analytics company, uses this pattern to let its trending-topics API route traffic to different Lambda function versions during development, testing, and production. The dev stage variable points to the dev alias of the ingestion function, the test stage variable points to the test alias, and the prod stage variable points to the prod alias. When Northbridge Works publishes a new Lambda version, the team updates only the alias to point to the new version, without touching the API Gateway configuration or breaking client-facing endpoints.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-override-request-response-parameters.html

Question 5Incorrect

The database engineering team at Everstone Ventures, a museum and cultural heritage foundation headquartered in Boston, is planning to migrate its ticketing and collections management application to AWS Cloud from an on-premises data center.

The team is evaluating Amazon RDS as the database tier for this application. Which of the following statements are correct regarding Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments? (Select TWO.)

Correct selection
RDS applies OS updates by performing maintenance on the standby, then promoting the standby to primary, and finally performing maintenance on the old primary, which becomes the new standby

Explanation

Correct. During a Multi-AZ maintenance event, Amazon RDS first patches the standby instance. Amazon RDS then promotes that patched standby instance to become the new primary instance. Amazon RDS then patches the old primary instance, and the old primary instance becomes the new standby instance. This sequence keeps downtime low during operating system updates. Keyword tip: this "patch standby, promote standby, patch old primary" sequence is the defining behavior of Multi-AZ maintenance.
Your selection is correct
Amazon RDS automatically initiates a failover to the standby in case the primary database fails for any reason

Explanation

Correct. One core purpose of Multi-AZ is automatic failover. If the primary DB instance becomes unavailable due to an Availability Zone outage or an instance failure, Amazon RDS automatically switches to the standby instance. This switch happens without manual intervention, and downtime is limited to the failover duration. Keyword tip: "automatic failover with no manual administration" is the hallmark benefit of Multi-AZ.
For automated backups, I/O activity is suspended on your primary DB since backups are not taken from the standby DB

Explanation

Incorrect. In a Multi-AZ deployment, Amazon RDS takes automated backups and snapshots from the standby instance, not the primary instance. Because backups come from the standby instance, I/O activity on the primary instance is not suspended during the backup window, so the primary instance avoids a performance impact. Keyword tip: "no I/O suspension during backups" is a specific availability benefit that exists precisely because backups come from the standby instance, not the primary instance.
To enhance read scalability, a Multi-AZ standby instance can be used to serve read requests

Explanation

Incorrect. A Multi-AZ standby instance cannot serve read traffic. Multi-AZ deployments exist to provide high availability and durability. The standby instance stays passive. The standby instance cannot answer queries until a failover happens. Keyword tip: if an option connects Multi-AZ to "read scalability" or "read replica," the option is describing Read Replicas, not Multi-AZ, and the option is incorrect.
Your selection is incorrect
Updates to your DB instance are asynchronously replicated across the Availability Zone to the standby in order to keep both in sync

Explanation

Incorrect. Replication between the primary instance and the standby instance in a Multi-AZ deployment is synchronous, not asynchronous. Synchronous replication keeps the standby instance fully up to date, so the standby instance can take over immediately during a failover. Keyword tip: Multi-AZ means synchronous replication for availability; asynchronous replication is instead associated with cross-region Read Replicas.

Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments provide high availability and durability through a synchronously replicated standby instance placed in a different Availability Zone. Multi-AZ gives automatic failover when the primary instance fails, and Multi-AZ reduces maintenance and backup impact because Amazon RDS performs patching and backups against the standby instance rather than the primary instance. Multi-AZ should not be confused with Read Replicas: Read Replicas use asynchronous replication and exist specifically for read scalability, not for availability. When a scenario asks about minimizing downtime during failures or maintenance windows without manual intervention, Multi-AZ is the correct feature; when a scenario asks about offloading read traffic or scaling reads, Read Replicas are the correct choice.

Applied example: Everstone Ventures runs a ticketing and collections management application that must stay available during museum operating hours, including weekends and holiday exhibitions. By deploying Amazon RDS in Multi-AZ mode, the database engineering team ensures that an Availability Zone outage or instance failure triggers an automatic failover to the synchronously replicated standby instance, keeping ticket sales and collection lookups running with minimal disruption to visitors and staff.

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/rds/faqs/

Question 6Incorrect

Overlook Collective needs to filter AWS X-Ray trace results using filter expressions on specific key-value pairs attached to custom subsegments, so its engineering team can quickly diagnose slow requests in its digital archive platform. As a museum and cultural heritage foundation headquartered in Boston that generates a high volume of X-Ray trace data from interactive exhibit kiosks and online collection searches, the foundation's developer must determine how to add these key-value pairs to the custom subsegments so they can later be filtered.

How should the developer add the key-value pairs to the custom subsegments?

Add metadata to the custom subsegments

Explanation

Incorrect. A developer can add metadata to a custom subsegment. AWS X-Ray does not index metadata values. Because metadata is not indexed, it cannot be used in filter expressions. Keyword tip: metadata is for storing extra data that the trace should keep, but that does not need to be searched.
Set up sampling for the custom subsegments

Explanation

Incorrect. Sampling controls what percentage of requests AWS X-Ray records and sends for analysis. Sampling manages cost and trace volume. Sampling has no effect on whether custom key-value data can be attached to subsegments or indexed for filtering. Keyword tip: sampling rules relate to trace volume, not to trace content structure.
Your answer is incorrect
Add the key-value pairs to the Trace ID

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS X-Ray does not allow a developer to attach custom key-value pairs to a Trace ID. A Trace ID is a system-generated identifier. A Trace ID is not a storage location for custom searchable data. Keyword tip: if an answer option describes modifying the Trace ID itself, treat that option as a fabricated distractor.
Correct answer
Add annotations to the custom subsegments

Explanation

Correct. Annotations are indexed key-value pairs that a developer can add to segments or custom subsegments. AWS X-Ray supports string, number, and Boolean values for annotations. Annotations are specifically designed to work with filter expressions and the GetTraceSummaries API. Keyword tip: whenever a scenario describes filtering or searching traces by custom data, annotations are the required mechanism because they are the only indexed option.

AWS X-Ray supports two ways to attach custom data to segments and subsegments: annotations and metadata. Annotations are indexed key-value pairs, and AWS X-Ray stores annotation values as string, number, or Boolean types. A developer can use annotations directly in filter expressions and in the GetTraceSummaries API to search for specific traces. Metadata supports richer or larger data structures, but AWS X-Ray does not index metadata, so a developer cannot use metadata in filter expressions; sampling and Trace IDs have no role in attaching or indexing custom searchable data, which makes them clear distractors in this scenario.

Use case: A museum and cultural heritage foundation like Overlook Collective might add an annotation such as "exhibitId" or "kioskLocation" to custom subsegments in its digital archive platform. The engineering team can then use a filter expression to quickly find every trace linked to a specific exhibit kiosk that is experiencing slow response times. This targeted filtering lets the team isolate performance problems without manually scanning through unrelated trace data.

References:

Question 7Correct

A recent spike in course enrollment traffic caused response times for read-heavy content queries to degrade noticeably. After investigating the root cause, the database team at Dunmore Alliance, an e-learning platform, decided to migrate its on-premises MySQL database to Amazon RDS.

The database workload is very read-heavy, and the team wants to refactor the application code to achieve optimum read performance for queries.

How can this objective be met?

Use Amazon RDS with a Multi-AZ deployment

Explanation

Incorrect. A Multi-AZ deployment creates a standby database instance in a different Availability Zone. This standby instance uses synchronous replication and exists for high availability and automatic failover, not for handling read traffic. The standby instance is not available to serve read queries in standard RDS engines. Keyword tip: Multi-AZ means disaster recovery and failover; read replicas mean read scaling.
Add database retries to the code and vertically scale the Amazon RDS database

Explanation

Incorrect. Vertical scaling means increasing the size of a single database instance. This approach does not distribute read traffic across multiple database endpoints, and it eventually hits a ceiling based on the largest available instance class. Retries do not solve a throughput problem; retries only handle temporary failures. Keyword tip: vertical scaling is a short-term fix for capacity, not a strategy for elastic read scaling.
Add a connection string to use a read replica on an Amazon EC2 instance

Explanation

Incorrect. An Amazon RDS read replica is a managed feature of the RDS service. RDS does not support attaching a read replica to a self-managed database running on an Amazon EC2 instance. To scale reads with RDS, the replica must also be provisioned as an RDS DB instance. Keyword tip: watch for distractors that combine a managed RDS feature with unmanaged EC2 compute as the target.
Your answer is correct
Add a connection string to use an Amazon RDS read replica for read queries

Explanation

Correct. Amazon RDS read replicas use the database engine's built-in asynchronous replication to keep one or more read-only copies of the primary DB instance. The application code sends write queries to the primary instance and sends read queries to a separate connection string that points to the read replica. This routing lets Dunmore Alliance scale read throughput horizontally, beyond what a single database instance can handle. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes a read-heavy workload and asks how to scale reads, think read replicas.

Amazon RDS offers two features that are easy to confuse: read replicas and Multi-AZ deployments. Read replicas create additional read-only copies of a database using asynchronous replication, and they exist specifically to scale out read-heavy workloads by letting the application send read queries to a separate endpoint. Multi-AZ deployments create a synchronously replicated standby instance in a different Availability Zone, and they exist specifically for high availability and automatic failover during an outage, not for handling extra read traffic. The correct choice depends on identifying whether the stated requirement is about read throughput (read replicas) or about availability and resilience (Multi-AZ), and on remembering that RDS-managed replication features cannot be recreated using self-managed EC2 instances.

A similar situation: an e-learning platform like Dunmore Alliance often sees traffic spikes when new courses launch or enrollment deadlines approach, and most of that traffic is read-only requests for course content and student progress data. Adding one or more Amazon RDS read replicas lets the platform route these read queries away from the primary database instance, which keeps write operations like grade updates and enrollment records fast and unaffected by the read load.

Question 8Correct

Quarrystone Alliance needs to run a serverless data store service using two Docker containers that must share resources, such as CPU, memory, and networking, with each other, as it modernizes the trip-planning backend for a public transportation authority operating a large metropolitan rail network.

Which of the following Amazon ECS configurations can be used to facilitate this use case?

Put the two containers into a single task definition using an EC2 launch type

Explanation

Incorrect. A single task definition does allow the two containers to share resources. However, the EC2 launch type still requires the team to provision, patch, and manage a cluster of EC2 instances. This management burden is the opposite of a serverless architecture. Keyword tip: whenever a scenario specifies "serverless," rule out the EC2 launch type and choose Fargate instead.
Your answer is correct
Put the two containers into a single task definition using a Fargate launch type

Explanation

Correct. Amazon ECS lets a single task definition contain multiple containers. Containers in the same task definition can share the task's network namespace, so they can talk to each other over localhost. These containers can also share storage volumes and the CPU and memory allocated to the task. The Fargate launch type removes the need to provision or manage EC2 instances, which satisfies the serverless requirement. Keyword tip: the words "serverless" and "share resources" together point to "single task definition" combined with the "Fargate launch type."
Put the two containers into two separate task definitions using a Fargate launch type

Explanation

Incorrect. Splitting the containers into two separate task definitions means each container runs in its own isolated task. Isolated tasks cannot share the network namespace or storage volumes with each other. The Fargate launch type does satisfy the serverless requirement, but the separation of task definitions fails the resource-sharing requirement. Keyword tip: containers must sit in the same task definition to share resources, no matter which launch type is used.
Put the two containers into two separate task definitions using an EC2 launch type

Explanation

Incorrect. Two separate task definitions produce two independently scheduled tasks. These tasks do not share the same network namespace, storage volumes, or resource allocation. The EC2 launch type also requires the team to provision and manage EC2 instances, which does not meet the serverless requirement. Keyword tip: "separate task definitions" always breaks resource sharing between containers, and the "EC2 launch type" is never the serverless choice.

This question tests understanding of how Amazon ECS task definitions and launch types work together. A single task definition can group multiple containers so they share the task's network namespace, storage volumes, and allocated CPU and memory. This sharing is required whenever containers need to communicate directly or exchange data closely. The Fargate launch type should be chosen whenever a scenario calls for a serverless, infrastructure-free deployment, while the EC2 launch type is appropriate only when the team needs direct control over the underlying compute instances. The correct option must satisfy two independent requirements at the same time: resource sharing, which requires a single task definition, and serverless infrastructure, which requires the Fargate launch type.

Practical example: Quarrystone Alliance runs a lightweight in-memory data store alongside a small sidecar container that handles cache warming for real-time bus and train arrival predictions. By placing both containers in one Fargate task definition, the sidecar can write directly to the data store container over localhost without any extra networking setup, and the transportation authority avoids managing any EC2 capacity for this workload.

Question 9Incorrect

Kingsford Consolidated, a petrochemical company, deploys an application automatically using AWS Elastic Beanstalk. The YAML configuration files are stored in the .ebextensions folder, and new files are frequently added or updated. The DevOps team at Kingsford Consolidated does not want to redeploy the application every time a configuration change occurs.

Instead, they want to manage configuration externally, securely, and have it load dynamically into the application at runtime.

Which option allows this?

Correct answer
Use SSM Parameter Store

Explanation

Correct. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store provides secure, hierarchical storage for configuration data and secrets. Parameter Store can hold values such as passwords, database connection strings, and license codes. The application can query Parameter Store through the AWS SDK or the AWS CLI at runtime. This design lets Kingsford Consolidated update configuration values without redeploying the application. Keyword tip: The phrase "externally managed, secure, dynamically loaded configuration without redeployment" points directly to Parameter Store.
Use Stage Variables

Explanation

Incorrect. Stage variables belong to Amazon API Gateway. Stage variables control settings for different deployment stages of an API. For example, a stage variable can point an API stage to a specific Lambda function alias. Stage variables have no connection to AWS Elastic Beanstalk configuration management. Keyword tip: Whenever a question mentions "stage variables," think of API Gateway stage configuration, not application deployment configuration.
Use S3

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 can store configuration files that an application reads at runtime, removing the need to manage servers. However, S3 does not provide security features by default; a team must explicitly configure encryption, versioning, and access control. Building a secure, hierarchical configuration system on S3 requires significant custom engineering effort. Keyword tip: When a scenario asks for built-in security and minimal setup for configuration or secrets, prefer Parameter Store over a custom S3-based solution.
Your answer is incorrect
Use Environment Variables

Explanation

Incorrect. Environment variables can pass configuration values to an application. However, Elastic Beanstalk environment variables are not encrypted at rest. Environment variables appear in clear text in the AWS Management Console and in some Elastic Beanstalk API responses. The scenario requires secure storage of configuration data, so environment variables do not meet this requirement. Keyword tip: Environment variables work well for simple, non-sensitive configuration, but they are not a secure secrets-management mechanism.

This question tests the concept of externalizing and securely managing application configuration outside the deployment package, which decouples configuration changes from code deployments. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is the correct choice because it offers secure, encrypted, hierarchical storage that an application can query dynamically at runtime through the SDK or CLI, without triggering a new deployment. Amazon S3 can technically store configuration files, but it lacks built-in encryption and access control for this use case and requires extra custom setup to reach the same security level. Elastic Beanstalk environment variables are not encrypted and are visible in plain text, and API Gateway stage variables apply only to API Gateway, not to Elastic Beanstalk, so neither option meets the requirement for secure, dynamic configuration management.

Consider this scenario: Kingsford Consolidated, a petrochemical company, runs safety-critical monitoring software on Elastic Beanstalk and needs to update sensor calibration thresholds and third-party API credentials without redeploying the application. By storing these values in Parameter Store, the DevOps team can update a parameter and have the running application read the new value on its next lookup, avoiding downtime and redeployment risk.

Question 10Incorrect

A recent load test on a public web portal revealed that client session data was lost whenever an Amazon EC2 instance was terminated by Auto Scaling during a traffic spike triggered by a major storm event. Yellowpine Trust, a weather and climate research agency headquartered in Denver, needs to redesign its session-handling architecture so that no session data is lost if an EC2 instance fails.

Which approach should the Developer implement to ensure that no session data is lost if an Amazon EC2 instance fails?

Your answer is incorrect
Use sticky sessions with an Elastic Load Balancer target group

Explanation

Incorrect. Sticky sessions bind a client to one specific EC2 instance. All requests from that client go to the same instance. Sticky sessions do not save session data anywhere outside that instance. If the instance fails, the session data stored on that instance is lost. Keyword tip: sticky sessions solve routing affinity, not data durability.
Use Elastic Load Balancer connection draining to stop sending requests to failing instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Connection draining lets an Elastic Load Balancer finish sending in-flight requests to an instance before removing that instance from service. Connection draining helps during planned scaling or deployment events. Connection draining does not save or protect session data. Keyword tip: connection draining manages graceful instance removal, not session data persistence.
Correct answer
Use Amazon DynamoDB to perform scalable session handling

Explanation

Correct. Amazon DynamoDB stores session data outside the EC2 instances, in a shared, durable, and highly available data store. If one EC2 instance fails, the session data remains available in DynamoDB and can be read by any other instance. This pattern, such as the DynamoDB Session Handler for PHP, is the standard best practice for building stateless, fault-tolerant web tiers behind a load balancer. Keyword tip: when a question asks how to protect session data from instance failure, look for answers that move session state to a shared external store such as DynamoDB or Amazon ElastiCache.
Use Amazon SQS to save session data

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS is a message queuing service. Amazon SQS is designed to decouple application components and buffer asynchronous workloads. Amazon SQS is not designed to store client session data. Keyword tip: SQS appears in questions about decoupling and asynchronous processing, not session state storage.

This question tests the concept of designing a stateless compute tier for fault tolerance. Application servers should not store session state locally, because any EC2 instance can fail or be replaced at any time in an auto-scaled, load-balanced environment. Sticky sessions control traffic routing, and connection draining controls graceful instance removal, but neither approach protects session data from being lost when an instance fails unexpectedly. Amazon SQS is a message queue and is not built for session storage. The correct pattern is to externalize session state to a shared, durable, low-latency data store such as Amazon DynamoDB or Amazon ElastiCache, so every instance can read and write the same session data.

Practical example: Yellowpine Trust runs a public weather-alert portal that must stay available during severe storm events, when EC2 instances scale up and down rapidly to handle sudden traffic spikes. By storing session data in DynamoDB instead of on individual EC2 instances, Yellowpine Trust ensures that a meteorologist's active session survives even if the instance serving their request is terminated during a scaling event.

Question 11Incorrect

Millbrook Dynamics, a logistics and freight company, runs its freight-tracking application on an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment configured with a Rolling deployment policy, which updates instances in batches to minimize downtime during releases. During a recent deployment, only two batches completed the update successfully, while the remaining batches failed to deploy the updated application version.

The development team manually terminates the instances that were part of the failed deployment batches.

What will happen to these terminated instances after Elastic Beanstalk replaces them?

Correct answer
Elastic Beanstalk will replace the failed instances with instances running the application version from the most recent successful deployment

Explanation

Correct. In a Rolling deployment, Elastic Beanstalk updates instances in batches. Elastic Beanstalk detaches each batch from the load balancer, deploys the new application version to that batch, and reattaches the batch to the load balancer. If a deployment fails partway through, the batches that already completed the update keep running the new version, while the batches that have not been updated yet keep running the old version. When the failed instances are terminated, the Auto Scaling group behind the Elastic Beanstalk environment replaces them using the most recently successfully deployed application version. Keyword tip: 'terminated failed batch instances get replaced with the latest successful version' is the defining behavior of Rolling deployments in Elastic Beanstalk.
Your answer is incorrect
Elastic Beanstalk will replace the failed instances only after the application version to be installed is manually chosen from the AWS Management Console

Explanation

Incorrect. Elastic Beanstalk does not ask an administrator to manually choose an application version in the AWS Management Console before replacing terminated instances. The replacement process is automatic and uses the most recently successfully deployed application version. Keyword tip: manual console selection is not part of the automatic replacement process that the Auto Scaling group performs.
Elastic Beanstalk will replace the failed instances with instances running the application version from the oldest successful deployment

Explanation

Incorrect. Elastic Beanstalk does not use the oldest successful batch as the reference for replacement instances. Elastic Beanstalk always uses the most recently completed successful batch to determine the application version for replacement instances. Keyword tip: when a question asks about the version used for replacement instances in a Rolling deployment, the correct answer is always the most recent successful batch, not the oldest one.
Elastic Beanstalk will not replace the failed instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Every Elastic Beanstalk environment is backed by an Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group automatically replaces terminated instances to keep the environment at its desired capacity. Elastic Beanstalk does not leave terminated instances unreplaced. Keyword tip: Auto Scaling group membership always implies automatic instance replacement.

Elastic Beanstalk's Rolling deployment policy updates instances in batches. Elastic Beanstalk detaches each batch from the load balancer, deploys the new application version to that batch, and reattaches the batch to the load balancer. If a batch fails, Elastic Beanstalk stops the deployment process, but the instances in batches that already completed the update keep running the new version. Elastic Beanstalk's underlying Auto Scaling group treats terminated instances as a capacity gap and replaces them using the most recently successfully deployed application version, not the oldest version and not the version that was running before the deployment started.

In practice: Millbrook Dynamics relies on this behavior to keep its freight-tracking fleet of instances consistent after a partial deployment failure. When the operations team terminates the failed instances, Elastic Beanstalk automatically replaces them with instances running the last successful application version, so the fleet does not fall back to outdated code and dispatch operations continue without manual intervention.

Brightwater Alliance needs to launch a scalable user management system with self-service log-in and sign-up capabilities that also enforces Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), in order to protect proprietary machine learning models that score buyer and seller trust levels across its online marketplace platform.

The engineering team, which is small and wants to avoid building and maintaining custom authentication infrastructure, must minimize development effort while meeting these requirements. Which of the following options can be used to implement a solution with the LEAST amount of development effort? (Select TWO.)

Your selection is correct
Use Amazon Cognito for user management and to facilitate the log-in/sign-up process

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Cognito is a fully managed service. Amazon Cognito provides a user directory called a user pool. This user pool lets developers add sign-up and sign-in features to an application with very little code. Amazon Cognito scales automatically to millions of users and supports federation with social and enterprise identity providers, so the team does not need to build or maintain custom authentication infrastructure. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for fast, low-effort, scalable user management with log-in and sign-up, choose Amazon Cognito user pools.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon RDS to create a custom solution for user management

Explanation

Incorrect. A custom solution built with AWS Lambda and Amazon RDS has the same problem as the AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB option. The team would need to build authentication, session management, password storage, and MFA from scratch. Building these features from scratch does not satisfy the requirement of minimal development effort. Keyword tip: a custom relational-database-backed authentication system signals high implementation overhead compared to a managed identity service.
Use AWS Lambda functions and Amazon DynamoDB to create a custom solution for user management

Explanation

Incorrect. A custom solution built with AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB would require the team to implement sign-up, sign-in, password management, MFA, and security hardening from scratch. Building all of these features from scratch directly contradicts the requirement for the least development effort. Keyword tip: any option that describes a fully custom-built authentication system signals high development effort, so favor managed identity services instead.
Your selection is correct
Use Amazon Cognito to enable Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) when users log in

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Cognito user pools include native support for Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA). A developer can enable SMS-based or Time-based One-Time Password (TOTP) MFA for users during sign-in through configuration, without writing custom MFA code. Keyword tip: when a scenario needs MFA added to a login flow with low development effort, choose the built-in MFA feature in Amazon Cognito.
Use Amazon SNS to send a Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) code via SMS to mobile app users

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SNS is a messaging and notification service. Amazon SNS does not generate, validate, or manage Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) codes for application users. If the team used Amazon SNS alone, the team would still need to build the MFA logic, code generation, validation, and expiration handling manually. Building this logic manually increases development effort instead of reducing it. Keyword tip: Amazon SNS sends messages, but Amazon SNS does not provide built-in MFA workflow logic for application users.

This question tests whether a candidate can recognize that Amazon Cognito is a managed identity service that minimizes development effort for user sign-up, sign-in, and MFA, compared to building a custom authentication system with AWS Lambda and a database. Amazon Cognito user pools should be used whenever a scenario calls for scalable, low-effort user directory management with built-in security features such as MFA. A custom Lambda-based solution should only be considered when Cognito's built-in capabilities cannot meet a highly specific business requirement. The core decision logic is this: a managed service such as Amazon Cognito reduces implementation and maintenance burden compared to a custom-built solution using AWS Lambda with Amazon DynamoDB or Amazon RDS, and Amazon SNS is a messaging tool, not an authentication or MFA orchestration service.

A similar situation: an online marketplace like Brightwater Alliance needs to onboard buyers and sellers quickly while protecting the proprietary trust-scoring models that rely on user account data. Instead of assigning engineers to build and maintain a custom login and MFA system, Brightwater Alliance can configure Amazon Cognito user pools in days, enabling secure sign-up, sign-in, and MFA with minimal custom code, so the engineering team can focus on the marketplace's core machine learning features.

Question 13Correct

Everstone Partners needs to ensure that all future log entries written to an existing Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group are encrypted with an AWS KMS customer master key (CMK), in order to meet updated data-protection requirements for its media streaming platform. This particular log group has been actively collecting video playback and content-delivery diagnostics for the past six months, and the company cannot recreate the log group without losing continuity of its monitoring dashboards.

How can the company achieve this?

Use the AWS CLI create-log-group command and specify the KMS key ARN

Explanation

Incorrect. The create-log-group command lets you specify a KMS key ARN only when you create a brand-new log group. Everstone Partners already has an existing log group, so this command cannot add encryption to it. Use create-log-group only when you are creating a log group for the first time. Keyword tip: 'create' commands apply only to new resources, not to resources that already exist.
Use the AWS CLI describe-log-groups command and specify the KMS key ARN

Explanation

Incorrect. The describe-log-groups command only returns information about existing log groups. This command does not attach a new KMS key to a log group. Use this command to check whether a log group already has a CMK associated with it, not to add one. Keyword tip: any AWS CLI command that starts with 'describe' is read-only and never modifies a resource.
Enable the encrypt feature on the log group via the CloudWatch Logs console

Explanation

Incorrect. The CloudWatch Logs console does not include an option to enable AWS KMS encryption on a log group. This limitation applies both when you create the log group and after the log group already exists. You can only configure this encryption through the AWS CLI, SDKs, or the CloudWatch Logs API. Keyword tip: treat any answer that mentions enabling encryption through the console as incorrect, because CloudWatch Logs does not offer that console feature.
Your answer is correct
Use the AWS CLI associate-kms-key command and specify the KMS key ARN

Explanation

Correct. The associate-kms-key command attaches a customer master key (CMK) to a log group that already exists. You do not need to recreate the log group to use this command. After you run this command, CloudWatch Logs encrypts all new log data with the CMK, while data stored before running the command stays in its original encryption state. Keyword tip: 'associate-kms-key' is the specific CLI command that adds or changes KMS encryption on a log group that already exists.

This question tests knowledge of how encryption at rest works for Amazon CloudWatch Logs when AWS KMS is layered on top of the default encryption. CloudWatch Logs always encrypts log data by default, but you can add KMS-based encryption in two ways: specify a KMS key ARN with create-log-group when you create a new log group, or use associate-kms-key to add or change the KMS key on a log group that already exists. The describe-log-groups command only reports the current configuration and cannot change it, and the CloudWatch Logs console does not expose any encryption toggle at all. The key decision point is whether the log group is new or already exists: a new log group uses create-log-group, while an existing log group requires associate-kms-key.

Consider this scenario: Everstone Partners, a media streaming company, has an existing CloudWatch Logs log group that has collected six months of video playback diagnostics. The security team wants all future log entries encrypted with a CMK, but the operations team cannot afford to recreate the log group because that would break existing monitoring dashboards. Running associate-kms-key on the existing log group lets the company add KMS encryption for future data without any disruption to historical data or existing tooling.

Question 14Incorrect

A performance audit triggered by a holiday shopping traffic surge revealed that a REST API deployed in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer was experiencing elevated read latency. The API stores transaction payloads in DynamoDB and serves static content through Amazon S3.

Traffic analysis showed that 80% of the read requests return data shared across all users. Thornfield Commission, a payment processing company headquartered in Dublin that operates this API, needs to improve application performance while optimizing cost with the least development effort.

As a developer, which approach should be used?

Enable ElastiCache for Redis for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon ElastiCache for Redis can act as a cache in front of DynamoDB. However, using ElastiCache for Redis requires the application to implement caching logic. This logic includes cache-aside handling, cache invalidation, and client-side integration. This approach needs more development effort than DAX. DAX requires no code changes, because DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB. Keyword tip: when a question asks for caching DynamoDB reads with minimal development effort, choose DAX instead of a general-purpose ElastiCache cluster.
Enable ElastiCache for Redis for DynamoDB and ElastiCache for Memcached for S3

Explanation

Incorrect. This option combines two caching services, ElastiCache for Redis and ElastiCache for Memcached. Neither service is optimal for this scenario. ElastiCache for Redis in front of DynamoDB requires custom integration work. ElastiCache for Memcached cannot cache or serve static content from S3, because delivering content at scale requires a content delivery network. Keyword tip: ElastiCache products cache database or application data in memory, but ElastiCache products are not designed to sit in front of object storage like S3.
Correct answer
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a fully managed, in-memory cache built specifically for DynamoDB. DAX can deliver up to a 10x performance improvement for read-heavy workloads. This improvement fits the scenario, because 80% of the reads return data shared across all users. DAX is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so no functional code changes are needed, which minimizes development effort. Pairing DAX with CloudFront to cache and distribute the static content from S3 at edge locations further improves performance and reduces cost, because delivering content from CloudFront edge caches is typically cheaper and faster than serving content directly from S3. Keyword tip: DAX is a drop-in DynamoDB read cache that needs no code changes; CloudFront is a CDN for S3 static content that uses edge caching.
Your answer is incorrect
Enable DAX for DynamoDB and ElastiCache for Memcached for S3

Explanation

Incorrect. DAX is the correct service to accelerate DynamoDB reads with minimal development effort. However, ElastiCache for Memcached cannot cache or serve static content stored in Amazon S3. ElastiCache for Memcached is an in-memory key-value store designed to sit in front of databases, not to deliver content. Keyword tip: to serve and cache static S3 content globally with low latency, use Amazon CloudFront, not ElastiCache.

This question tests the ability to match a caching strategy to a specific data source in a read-heavy architecture. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is the purpose-built, in-memory cache for DynamoDB, and DAX is API-compatible with the DynamoDB API, so no application code changes are required to add caching. CloudFront is the purpose-built content delivery network for static content stored in Amazon S3, and CloudFront caches that content at edge locations to reduce latency and cost. ElastiCache for Redis or Memcached can also cache data, but ElastiCache requires custom cache-aside logic for DynamoDB and cannot function as a CDN for S3, so ElastiCache demands more development effort and does not fully solve the S3 caching need. The correct decision logic is to pick the lowest-effort, AWS-native caching service designed for each data source: DAX for DynamoDB reads, and CloudFront for S3 static content.

Real-world example: A payment processing company such as Thornfield Commission often serves shared reference data, for example currency exchange rates or merchant category codes, to every client that calls its transaction API. Enabling DAX in front of DynamoDB lets Thornfield Commission absorb sudden traffic spikes, such as a holiday shopping surge, without rewriting application code. Serving the associated static assets, such as receipt templates or fee schedule documents, through CloudFront in front of S3 keeps global latency low and infrastructure cost predictable during those spikes.

Question 15Incorrect

Everstone Dynamics needs to prevent occasional ThrottlingException errors from disrupting its disaster-relief coordination platform, a nonprofit organization that scales the platform to thousands of concurrent instances during large-scale relief efforts, causing frequent calls to an Amazon DynamoDB table that stores incident records. The platform is coded in a programming language for which no AWS SDK is available.

What can be done to prevent the errors from occurring?

Correct answer
Add exponential backoff to the application logic

Explanation

Correct. Exponential backoff is a retry strategy. Each failed retry waits longer than the previous one before trying again. This spacing reduces the rate of requests sent to the throttled DynamoDB table, which increases the chance that later retries succeed. AWS SDKs normally include this retry logic automatically. Because Everstone Dynamics uses a programming language with no supported AWS SDK, the retry-with-exponential-backoff logic must be written manually inside the application code. Keyword tip: when a question mentions ThrottlingException together with no available AWS SDK, exponential backoff implemented in application code is the correct fix.
Use Amazon SQS as an API message bus

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS is a message queue service. It decouples the component that sends a message from the component that processes it. SQS does not manage retries for direct, synchronous API calls to DynamoDB, so adding SQS here would add cost and complexity without fixing the throttling problem. Keyword tip: SQS decouples producers and consumers of messages; it does not add API-level retry logic.
Your answer is incorrect
Send the items to DynamoDB through Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivers streaming data to specific destinations. DynamoDB is not one of the destinations that Firehose supports. This option is not technically possible for writing items into a DynamoDB table. Keyword tip: remember that Firehose delivers to Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, and HTTP endpoints, not to DynamoDB directly.
Pass API calls through Amazon API Gateway

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon API Gateway is used to create, publish, and manage APIs for other clients to call. Placing API Gateway in front of the DynamoDB calls does not add retry logic to those calls. The ThrottlingException errors would still occur because the root cause, missing retry behavior, is not addressed. Keyword tip: API Gateway manages and exposes APIs; it does not implement client-side retry behavior.

This question tests knowledge of how to handle DynamoDB throttling when the AWS SDK, which normally provides built-in retry logic, is not available for the application's programming language. Exponential backoff is the standard fix for throttling. It spaces out retry attempts with progressively longer wait times, which reduces pressure on the table's read or write capacity. Other techniques that reduce throttling include spreading requests evenly across partition keys to avoid hot partitions, and adding a caching layer such as DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for read-heavy workloads. When you see a throttling error in a question, check first whether retry logic is missing before considering additional components like message queues or API gateways, because those components add complexity without fixing the root cause.

Applied example: Everstone Dynamics runs its disaster-relief coordination platform in a language without AWS SDK support. During a large-scale relief operation, thousands of application instances write incident records to DynamoDB at the same time, and some calls receive ThrottlingException errors. A developer adds a manual exponential backoff routine to the write logic. Each retry waits longer than the last, which lowers the request rate against the table and lets the relief data get written successfully without any additional AWS services.

AWS X-Ray

Question 17Correct

Riverstone Innovations needs to prevent customers from viewing each other's meter-reading and billing records inside a shared self-service portal. The company, a regional water utility that serves several municipalities, stores all customer account data in a single Amazon DynamoDB table to keep operations simple.

How can the Developer restrict access so that each customer can view only their own data?

Read records from DynamoDB and discard irrelevant data client-side

Explanation

Incorrect. Reading all records and removing irrelevant data on the client side wastes read capacity, because it reads more data than needed. It is also insecure, because sensitive data leaves DynamoDB and reaches the client device before it is discarded. This increases the risk that the data is exposed. The correct approach blocks unauthorized access on the server side, using IAM conditions, before data ever leaves DynamoDB. Keyword tip: any option describing client-side filtering of sensitive data is a security anti-pattern and should be marked incorrect.
Use an identity-based policy that restricts read access to the table to specific principals

Explanation

Incorrect. An identity-based policy without item-level conditions controls access to the entire table. It does not control access to individual items inside that table. If Riverstone Innovations grants read access this way, every permitted customer could see every other customer's records. The fix is to add a Condition element that scopes access down to specific primary key values. Keyword tip: a policy that grants or denies access at the table level, with no condition element mentioned, cannot achieve item-level isolation.
Use separate access keys for each customer to call the API and restrict access to specific items based on access key ID

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM policy condition cannot check the access key ID used to sign a request. An access key is only a credential tied to an IAM identity. A policy condition cannot reference the access key value itself. The correct method ties the condition to the caller's identity through dynamodb:LeadingKeys, not to access key values. Keyword tip: any option that asks to filter or restrict access by access key ID is not a valid IAM condition and should be treated as incorrect.
Your answer is correct
Restrict access to specific items based on certain primary key values

Explanation

Correct. IAM supports fine-grained access control for DynamoDB. A policy can use a Condition element to restrict access to specific items. This is often done with the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key, which maps a primary key value to the identity of the caller. This method is the recommended approach when many customers share one table and each customer must only reach their own items. Keyword tip: look for the terms "fine-grained access control" or "LeadingKeys" as signals for this pattern.

This question tests fine-grained access control in Amazon DynamoDB using IAM policy Condition elements. A Condition element can scope permissions down to specific items or attributes based on primary key values. This is commonly implemented with the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition key, tied to the identity of the caller. Use this pattern whenever multiple users or tenants share one table and must be isolated from each other's data, without the cost of creating separate tables per tenant. A table-level identity-based policy without conditions only controls access to the whole table. Client-side filtering is inefficient and insecure, since it moves sensitive data to the client before removing it. The correct decision is always to enforce item-level isolation on the server side, using IAM conditions, whenever per-user data isolation is required inside a shared table.

Real-world example: Riverstone Innovations runs a customer self-service portal where residents across several municipalities check their own meter readings and billing history. All customer records live in one shared DynamoDB table to reduce operational overhead. By attaching an IAM policy with a dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition tied to each authenticated customer identity, Riverstone Innovations ensures that a customer in one municipality can never read the billing data belonging to a customer in another municipality, without needing a separate table per municipality.

Question 18Correct

Ulverstone Holdings needs to process a large batch of disaster-assessment files as quickly as possible using AWS Lambda. This nonprofit disaster-relief organization coordinates emergency response across multiple regions, and its Lambda function takes approximately 3 minutes to process each file and does not return any important data to the caller.

A developer at Ulverstone Holdings has written a script that will invoke the function using the AWS CLI.

What is the FASTEST way to process all the files?

Invoke the Lambda function asynchronously with the invocation type RequestResponse and process the files sequentially

Explanation

Incorrect. RequestResponse is the invocation type reserved for synchronous calls. RequestResponse cannot be paired with asynchronous invocation, so this combination is technically invalid. Even if it were valid, processing the files sequentially would still be slow. Keyword tip: if you see RequestResponse mentioned alongside the word "asynchronously," treat that combination as mismatched and incorrect.
Your answer is correct
Invoke the Lambda function asynchronously with the invocation type Event and process the files in parallel

Explanation

Correct. Setting the invocation type to Event triggers an asynchronous invocation. The AWS CLI returns immediately without waiting for the Lambda function to complete, so the script can send invocation requests for all files in parallel. AWS Lambda then processes these invocations concurrently, subject to concurrency limits, and handles retries internally. This combination is the fastest approach when the caller does not need the function's response. Keyword tip: the Event invocation type means asynchronous, fire-and-forget behavior, which is ideal for parallel fan-out workloads.
Invoke the Lambda function synchronously with the invocation type Event and process the files in parallel

Explanation

Incorrect. Event is the invocation type reserved for asynchronous calls. Pairing Event with synchronous invocation is technically invalid, because Event never waits for or returns a response. Keyword tip: if the word "synchronously" is paired with the Event invocation type, that combination is inherently inconsistent and therefore wrong.
Invoke the Lambda function synchronously with the invocation type RequestResponse and process the files sequentially

Explanation

Incorrect. Synchronous invocation with the RequestResponse type forces the caller to wait for each Lambda function to finish before the script can continue. Combined with sequential processing, this option becomes the slowest possible approach, because no invocation ever overlaps with another. Keyword tip: RequestResponse always means synchronous, blocking behavior, which is not optimal when the caller does not need the function's response.

This question tests understanding of AWS Lambda invocation types and when to use synchronous versus asynchronous invocation for performance. Synchronous invocation, using the RequestResponse type, blocks the caller until the function completes. Use synchronous invocation only when the caller needs the function's result immediately. Asynchronous invocation, using the Event type, returns control to the caller right away and lets Lambda manage execution and retries in the background. Use asynchronous invocation for fire-and-forget, high-throughput workloads where the caller does not need the output. When the caller does not need the function's output, invoking asynchronously and firing requests in parallel is always faster than invoking synchronously and waiting for each call to finish one at a time, because parallel asynchronous invocation removes the serialization bottleneck caused by waiting for each response.

Consider this scenario: Ulverstone Holdings needs to process thousands of disaster-assessment files immediately after a major flood or earthquake, so response teams can act on the data without delay. Because the Lambda function does not return any information the script needs to use, Ulverstone Holdings can invoke the function asynchronously with the Event type and send all invocation requests in parallel. This approach lets AWS Lambda process every file concurrently in the background, dramatically reducing the total time needed to complete disaster-assessment processing compared to waiting for each file to finish one at a time.

Question 19Correct

The platform engineering team at Fairmount Partners, an e-learning platform, is building a RESTful API service using Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda integration. The team must support different API versions for testing purposes before rolling out new course-content features to students.

Which of the following approaches is the best way to accomplish this?

Use an API Gateway Lambda authorizer to route API clients to the correct API version

Explanation

Incorrect. A Lambda authorizer is an API Gateway feature that uses a Lambda function to control access to an API. A Lambda authorizer typically implements a custom authorization scheme, such as OAuth, or checks request parameters to confirm caller identity. A Lambda authorizer controls authentication and authorization. A Lambda authorizer does not route requests to different API versions. Keyword tip: Lambda authorizer means custom access control or authentication, not version management.
Set up an API Gateway resource policy to identify the API versions and provide context to the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. An API Gateway resource policy is a JSON policy document attached to an API. A resource policy controls whether a specified principal, such as an IAM user or role, can invoke the API. A resource policy governs access control. A resource policy does not manage API versioning or route calls to different backend logic. Keyword tip: resource policy means who can call the API, not which version of the API gets called.
Use an X-Version header to identify which version is being called and pass that header to the Lambda function

Explanation

Incorrect. A custom header could signal which version a client wants, but API Gateway does not natively read a header to select a different backend integration or deployment. This approach would require Fairmount Partners to build custom routing logic inside the Lambda function itself, instead of using a built-in API Gateway mechanism. Keyword tip: a custom header like X-Version is a plausible-sounding but non-native approach; the AWS-native mechanism for API versioning is stages and stage variables.
Your answer is correct
Deploy the API versions as unique stages with unique endpoints and use stage variables to provide the context to identify the API versions

Explanation

Correct. A stage in Amazon API Gateway is a named reference to a deployment. A deployment is a snapshot of the API at a point in time. Stage variables are name-value pairs attached to a specific stage. Stage variables work like environment variables. The team can deploy each API version as its own stage with its own endpoint. The team can then use stage variables to set stage-specific configuration, such as which Lambda function alias to call. This lets Fairmount Partners test multiple versions of the same API, such as alpha, beta, and production, without duplicating the API definition. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes multiple deployment environments or versions of the same REST API with different backend configurations, the answer is stages plus stage variables.

This question tests knowledge of how to manage multiple versions of a REST API in Amazon API Gateway for testing and release management. Stages and stage variables are the AWS-native mechanism for this task. Each stage represents a separate deployment snapshot with its own endpoint. Stage variables act as environment-specific configuration, such as pointing to different Lambda function aliases, without duplicating the API definition. Lambda authorizers control authentication and authorization, resource policies control access based on the calling principal, and custom headers are not a built-in API Gateway versioning feature, so none of these three options replace the stages-plus-stage-variables approach.

Real-world example: at Fairmount Partners, the platform engineering team needs to test a new version of the course-enrollment API before releasing it to students. The team deploys the new version to a separate stage, such as "beta", while the current production version stays on the "prod" stage. Each stage has its own endpoint and its own stage variables pointing to the correct Lambda function alias, so the team can run tests against the beta stage without affecting students using the live platform.
