Question 20Correct

During a post-incident review of a brief customer-facing outage, the on-call engineering team at Kingsford Innovations, a telecommunications provider headquartered in Toronto, discovered that an Amazon EC2 instance flagged as unhealthy by the Elastic Load Balancer was never replaced by the Auto Scaling group backing the company's AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment, kingsford-network-portal-env. The environment runs a small number of EC2 instances behind the load balancer and Auto Scaling group.

As a developer investigating the root cause, which configuration should be implemented so that unhealthy instances are automatically replaced going forward?

Your answer is correct
The health check type of the instance's Auto Scaling group must be changed from EC2 to ELB by using a configuration file

Explanation

Correct. By default, an Auto Scaling group uses the EC2 health check type. The EC2 health check type only evaluates the instance's system and hardware status. The EC2 health check type does not evaluate the health of the application running on the instance. The load balancer, however, can detect application-level failures through its own health checks. To make the Auto Scaling group react to the load balancer's health check results, the health check type must be changed from EC2 to ELB. This change is typically made through an Elastic Beanstalk configuration file (.ebextensions) or directly in the Auto Scaling group settings. Keyword tip: when a load balancer marks an instance as unhealthy but the Auto Scaling group does not replace that instance, check whether the health check type is still set to EC2 instead of ELB.
The ping path field of the load balancer is configured incorrectly

Explanation

Incorrect. A misconfigured ping path causes the load balancer's health checks to fail for every instance in the target group, not just one instance. The load balancer applies the same health check configuration to all instances in a given target group. In this scenario, only one instance failed, so a misconfigured ping path does not explain the observed behavior. Keyword tip: a ping path or health check path misconfiguration produces failures across the entire fleet, not an isolated single-instance failure.
Health check parameters were configured to check instance health alone. The instance failed due to an application failure, which was not configured as a parameter for the health check status

Explanation

Incorrect. This statement describes a true limitation of the EC2 health check type: it only checks instance-level status, not application health. This statement does not describe a configuration fix. The statement only explains why the failure happened. It does not solve the problem in the scenario. Keyword tip: watch for answer options that only restate the cause of a problem without giving an action that fixes it.
The Auto Scaling group does not automatically replace unhealthy instances marked by the load balancer. They must be manually replaced from the AWS Management Console

Explanation

Incorrect. This statement is false. When an Auto Scaling group's health check type is set to ELB, the Auto Scaling group automatically replaces instances that the load balancer marks as unhealthy. Manual replacement through the AWS Management Console is not required in this case. Keyword tip: be suspicious of any answer option that claims AWS cannot automate a task that is documented as automatable.

This question tests knowledge of how Auto Scaling group health check types interact with Elastic Load Balancing in an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment. By default, an Auto Scaling group uses the EC2 health check type. The EC2 health check type only checks the instance's system status, not the application running on it. If an instance fails at the application level, the load balancer detects the failure, but the Auto Scaling group does not act on that failure unless the health check type is set to ELB. Changing the health check type to ELB, usually through an Elastic Beanstalk configuration file, makes the Auto Scaling group treat the load balancer's health check results as the source of truth for replacement decisions.

Practical example: Kingsford Innovations runs a customer support portal on Elastic Beanstalk. When the application layer crashes but the underlying EC2 instance keeps running, the load balancer correctly marks the instance as unhealthy. The Auto Scaling group ignores this signal because its health check type is still set to EC2. Switching the health check type to ELB lets the Auto Scaling group automatically terminate and replace the failing instance, restoring service without manual intervention.

Question 21Correct

After a post-incident review following a regional flood response, a nonprofit disaster-relief organization discovered that its volunteer coordination application, which runs across multiple EC2 instances and triggers AWS Lambda functions to generate automated damage-assessment reports, had no shared storage layer, causing inconsistent case files during the emergency. Elmsworth Group now needs a central file storage solution that scales on demand and can be used concurrently by multiple Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances and AWS Lambda functions.

Which storage solution will meet these requirements?

Create an Amazon EBS Multi-Attach volume.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EBS Multi-Attach lets a single Provisioned IOPS SSD volume attach to multiple EC2 instances at the same time. Amazon EBS Multi-Attach only works within a single Availability Zone. Amazon EBS Multi-Attach also requires a cluster-aware file system to manage concurrent writes safely. AWS Lambda functions cannot attach to or access an Amazon EBS volume at all. Keyword tip: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach is limited to EC2-to-EC2 block storage sharing, not compute-to-serverless file sharing.
Your answer is correct
Create an Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) file system.

Explanation

Correct. Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system. Amazon EFS automatically scales storage capacity up and down as files are added or removed, with no capacity planning required. Multiple EC2 instances can mount Amazon EFS at the same time, and AWS Lambda functions can also access Amazon EFS through the EFS integration for Lambda. This combination makes Amazon EFS the correct choice for shared, on-demand file storage across EC2 and Lambda. Keyword tip: the phrases shared file system, scales on demand, and accessible by EC2 and Lambda at the same time point directly to Amazon EFS.
Create an Amazon ElastiCache cluster.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon ElastiCache is an in-memory caching service. Amazon ElastiCache speeds up data retrieval for applications and databases. Amazon ElastiCache is not a file storage system. EC2 instances and Lambda functions cannot mount Amazon ElastiCache as a shared file system. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions in-memory caching or sub-millisecond data retrieval, think Amazon ElastiCache, not shared file storage.
Create an AWS Storage Gateway volume gateway.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Storage Gateway connects on-premises applications and infrastructure to AWS cloud storage. AWS Storage Gateway is built for hybrid cloud storage architectures. AWS Storage Gateway is not designed to act as a native shared file store for EC2 instances and Lambda functions in an all-cloud scenario. Keyword tip: words like hybrid, on-premises, or connect data center to AWS point to AWS Storage Gateway, not Amazon EFS.

This question tests the ability to choose the correct AWS storage service for shared, elastic file access across both server-based compute (EC2) and serverless compute (Lambda). Amazon EFS is the correct choice because it provides a fully elastic, NFS-based shared file system. Amazon EFS requires no capacity planning and supports concurrent access from EC2 instances, ECS containers, and Lambda functions at the same time. Amazon ElastiCache only handles in-memory caching, AWS Storage Gateway only connects on-premises systems to AWS cloud storage, and Amazon EBS Multi-Attach only shares block storage between EC2 instances within one Availability Zone, so none of these three options can meet the requirement for shared file access from both EC2 and Lambda.

A similar situation: a disaster-relief organization like Elmsworth Group could use Amazon EFS to store shared case files and damage-assessment reports. Field-response EC2 instances and automated Lambda functions could then read from and write to the same file system at the same time, with no manual capacity planning needed during a sudden surge in relief operations.

What occurs if the deployment of the new version fails?

The last known working deployment is automatically restored using the snapshot stored in Amazon S3

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy does not keep a snapshot of previous deployments in Amazon S3 for rollback purposes. Amazon S3 may store the application revision bundle used during deployment, but it is not used to restore a prior state. Keyword tip: if an option describes a rollback as restoring a stored snapshot, treat this as a warning sign, because CodeDeploy rollbacks work by redeploying a previous revision, not by restoring a snapshot.
AWS CodePipeline promotes the most recent working deployment with a SUCCEEDED status to production

Explanation

Incorrect. The scenario only describes AWS CodeDeploy with automatic rollback enabled. AWS CodePipeline is not part of this setup. CodePipeline does not automatically promote a prior successful deployment when a CodeDeploy deployment fails. Keyword tip: watch for answer options that introduce a service the scenario never mentions, since this is a common distractor pattern.
Correct answer
A new deployment of the last known working version of the application is deployed with a new deployment ID

Explanation

Correct. When automatic rollback is enabled and a deployment fails, AWS CodeDeploy responds by redeploying the last known good application revision. This redeployment is treated as a completely new deployment and receives its own new deployment ID. CodeDeploy does not restore the old deployment record; it creates a fresh one. Keyword tip: the phrase 'new deployment with a new deployment ID' is the defining signal for how CodeDeploy rollback works.
Your answer is incorrect
CodeDeploy switches the Route 53 alias records back to the known good green deployment and terminates the failed blue deployment

Explanation

Incorrect. Switching Route 53 alias records between a blue environment and a green environment describes a blue/green deployment pattern. This scenario describes a standard in-place deployment to EC2 instances with automatic rollback enabled, not a blue/green traffic-shifting setup. Keyword tip: only pick options about blue/green traffic shifting when the scenario explicitly states that a blue/green deployment type is configured.

This question tests how AWS CodeDeploy's automatic rollback feature behaves after a failed deployment. CodeDeploy does not restore a previous state from a stored snapshot, and it does not switch traffic using Route 53 aliases unless a blue/green deployment type is explicitly configured. Instead, CodeDeploy triggers a new deployment of the last known good application revision, and this new deployment gets its own unique deployment ID. Recognizing this redeploy-based rollback model helps distinguish CodeDeploy's in-place rollback behavior from blue/green traffic-shifting patterns and from AWS CodePipeline's separate role in release orchestration.

Consider this scenario: Brightwater Guild's DevOps team pushes a new billing platform release through CodeDeploy, and the release fails its post-deployment health checks. Because automatic rollback is enabled, CodeDeploy immediately redeploys the last stable version of the billing platform to the EC2 fleet, creating a new deployment ID for that rollback action so the team can track it separately in the deployment history. This behavior lets the utility company recover quickly from a bad release without manual intervention, while keeping a clear audit trail of every deployment attempt.

Which strategy should the team follow to create the Lambda deployment package?

Correct answer
Create a ZIP file with the source code and all dependent libraries

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda deployment package is a ZIP archive or a container image. The deployment package must contain both the function's source code and any dependent libraries that are not included in the base runtime. Lambda has no built-in mechanism to fetch or install packages at invocation time. Keyword tip: when a function needs libraries outside the native runtime, bundle those libraries directly into the ZIP file, or use a Lambda layer for libraries shared across multiple functions.
Create a ZIP file with the source code and a script that installs the dependent libraries at runtime

Explanation

Incorrect. Installing dependencies through a script at runtime adds significant cold-start latency to every invocation. This approach is not a supported or recommended pattern for Lambda. A Lambda function must be fully self-contained and ready to execute immediately after it starts. Keyword tip: any mention of installing packages at runtime signals an anti-pattern for Lambda dependency management.
Your answer is incorrect
Create a ZIP file with the source code and an appspec.yml file. Add the libraries to the appspec.yml file and upload it to Amazon S3. Deploy using AWS CloudFormation

Explanation

Incorrect. The appspec.yml file is a configuration file used by AWS CodeDeploy. AWS CodeDeploy uses appspec.yml to define deployment lifecycle hooks and traffic-shifting behavior. The appspec.yml file does not declare or bundle library dependencies. CloudFormation does not read or process appspec.yml; CodeDeploy does. Keyword tip: appspec.yml always points to AWS CodeDeploy, never to dependency packaging.
Create a ZIP file with the source code and a buildspec.yml file that installs the dependent libraries on AWS Lambda

Explanation

Incorrect. The buildspec.yml file is used by AWS CodeBuild. AWS CodeBuild uses buildspec.yml to define build phases, such as compiling code and running tests. A buildspec.yml file cannot install libraries directly inside a running Lambda function. A buildspec.yml file is not a substitute for including dependencies in the deployment package. Keyword tip: buildspec.yml always points to AWS CodeBuild build instructions, not to Lambda dependency installation.

This question tests understanding of how an AWS Lambda deployment package must be structured when a function depends on libraries outside the native runtime. The correct approach is to bundle the source code together with all required dependencies into a single ZIP archive, or to use a Lambda layer for libraries shared across functions, or to use a container image when the dependency set is large. Lambda cannot install packages dynamically when it receives an invocation. Files such as appspec.yml and buildspec.yml serve different purposes in a CI/CD pipeline: appspec.yml configures AWS CodeDeploy, and buildspec.yml configures AWS CodeBuild. Neither file manages Lambda function dependencies, so a packaging strategy should always keep the deployment artifact self-contained rather than deferring dependency resolution to runtime.

Business scenario: Ashgrove Foundation's application development team needs its imaging microservice to process high volumes of archival photographs reliably, without added latency from installing packages during each invocation. By packaging the required image-processing libraries directly into the Lambda ZIP archive, the team ensures every invocation starts with all dependencies already available, keeping the digitization pipeline fast and consistent for the foundation's collection.

Question 24Correct

The platform engineering team at Ironclad Guild, a ride-sharing platform, has configured inbound traffic rules for the relevant ports on both the security group of an Amazon EC2 instance and the network access control list (NACL) of the subnet in which the instance resides.

This instance hosts the company's real-time trip-dispatch service. Despite this configuration, the team is unable to connect to the service running on the EC2 instance.

As a developer associate, which of the following statements correctly identifies the root cause and the recommended fix for this issue?

Your answer is correct
Security groups are stateful, so allowing inbound traffic to the necessary ports enables the connection. Network ACLs are stateless, so you must allow both inbound and outbound traffic

Explanation

Correct. Security groups are stateful. A stateful security group automatically allows outbound return traffic once inbound traffic on a specific port is allowed, regardless of the outbound rules configured. Network ACLs are stateless. A stateless network ACL requires you to explicitly allow both the inbound traffic on the service port and the outbound traffic on the ephemeral port range (1024-65535) used for the return traffic. If the network ACL's outbound rules do not allow this range, the connection fails even when the security group is configured correctly. Keyword tip: when a security group looks correct but the connection still fails, check the network ACL's outbound ephemeral port rules first.
Rules associated with network ACLs should never be modified from the command line. An attempt to modify rules from the command line blocks the rule and results in erratic behavior

Explanation

Incorrect. This option describes a restriction that does not exist in AWS. Network ACL rules can be modified through the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, or an SDK. Modifying a rule from the command line does not cause erratic behavior. Keyword tip: if an option claims a specific management tool is forbidden for a core AWS resource, treat that claim as a sign of a fabricated distractor.
The IAM role defined in the security group is different from the IAM role that is given access in the network ACLs

Explanation

Incorrect. Security groups and network ACLs do not use IAM roles. Both services control traffic using rules based on IP addresses, ports, and protocols. IAM roles control identity-based permissions for AWS API actions, which is a separate and unrelated function. Keyword tip: any option that combines IAM roles with security groups or network ACLs is testing whether you know these are unrelated services, so treat it as a likely distractor.
Network ACLs are stateful, so allowing inbound traffic to the necessary ports enables the connection. Security groups are stateless, so you must allow both inbound and outbound traffic

Explanation

Incorrect. This option reverses the actual behavior of the two services. Network ACLs are stateless. A stateless network ACL requires you to explicitly allow return traffic on both inbound and outbound rules, including the ephemeral port range. Security groups are stateful. A stateful security group automatically allows return traffic without needing a matching outbound rule. Keyword tip: memorize the fixed pairing "security groups = stateful" and "network ACLs = stateless."

This question tests the difference between security groups and network ACLs in terms of statefulness, and how that difference affects return traffic for a connection. A security group is stateful: once inbound traffic is allowed on a specific port, the matching outbound return traffic is automatically permitted, regardless of the outbound rules configured. A network ACL is stateless: both inbound traffic on the service port and outbound traffic on the ephemeral port range (1024-65535) must be explicitly allowed, or the return traffic is blocked. When a security group is configured correctly but a connection still fails, the correct troubleshooting step is to check whether the subnet's network ACL is blocking the required outbound ephemeral port traffic.

In practice: at Ironclad Guild, a ride-sharing platform, the platform engineering team could face this exact issue when a dispatch service instance fails to receive driver location updates. The team would first confirm that the security group allows inbound traffic on the correct port, then check the subnet's network ACL to confirm that its outbound rules permit the ephemeral port range needed for return traffic. This distinction between stateful security groups and stateless network ACLs is a common root cause of connectivity problems in production dispatch systems that rely on constant, low-latency communication.

Question 25Incorrect

Kestrel Works, a semiconductor manufacturer, operates a customer-facing product documentation portal distributed through Amazon CloudFront, with an Application Load Balancer configured as the origin. Kestrel Works' engineering team wants visitors who request documentation pages that have been decommissioned to be automatically redirected to a current landing page instead of receiving a generic 404 error.

The team plans to attach an AWS Lambda@Edge function to the existing CloudFront distribution to implement this redirect logic, and the solution must minimize the number of Lambda@Edge invocations and associated resource consumption.

Which CloudFront event type should the team use to invoke the Lambda@Edge function that contains the redirect logic?

Origin request

Explanation

Incorrect. An origin-request trigger runs before CloudFront sends the request to the origin. At this point, CloudFront has not received any response from the origin. The Lambda@Edge function cannot see the 404 status code because the origin has not generated it yet. Keyword tip: use an origin-request trigger when the function needs to change the request before it reaches the origin, such as modifying the origin path or adding headers.
Your answer is incorrect
Viewer request

Explanation

Incorrect. A viewer-request trigger runs on every incoming request from the viewer, before CloudFront checks its cache. At this point, CloudFront has not yet contacted the origin, so the function cannot know whether the origin will return a 404 status code. Keyword tip: use a viewer-request trigger for tasks that must happen before the cache lookup, such as authentication or header-based routing decisions.
Correct answer
Origin response

Explanation

Correct. An origin-response trigger runs after CloudFront receives the HTTP response from the origin server. At this point, the Lambda@Edge function can read the 404 status code that the Application Load Balancer returned. The function can then replace that response with a redirect response, such as an HTTP 301 or 302 status code. CloudFront can cache this modified response, so the Lambda@Edge function does not run again for the same request, which keeps resource usage low. Keyword tip: use an origin-response trigger whenever the function must inspect or change the status code or body that came from the origin.
Viewer response

Explanation

Incorrect. A viewer-response trigger runs on every response sent to the viewer, including responses served directly from the CloudFront cache. This trigger would invoke the Lambda@Edge function far more often than necessary, because it also runs for cached content that never needed a redirect. Keyword tip: avoid a viewer-response trigger when the goal is to minimize invocations and the redirect logic only depends on the origin's response, not on every cached response.

CloudFront supports four Lambda@Edge trigger points: viewer request, origin request, origin response, and viewer response. The correct trigger depends on when the needed data becomes available in the request-response cycle. Viewer-request and origin-request triggers run before CloudFront receives any response from the origin, so they cannot see a 404 status code. Origin-response triggers run right after CloudFront receives the origin's response, so they can inspect and replace that response, and CloudFront can cache the result to avoid repeated invocations. Viewer-response triggers run on every response, including cached ones, which increases invocations and resource use without adding value for this use case.

A similar situation: A semiconductor manufacturer like Kestrel Works often retires outdated product datasheets and technical bulletins as new chip revisions are released. Using an origin-response Lambda@Edge trigger lets Kestrel Works redirect visitors away from decommissioned documentation pages efficiently, while CloudFront's caching of the modified response keeps Lambda@Edge invocation counts, and therefore cost, to a minimum.

Question 26Correct

A recent load test revealed that the streaming application must handle at least 10,000 requests per minute during peak listening hours, exposing a scalability issue in how session data is stored. The web tier at Saltmarsh Holdings, a music streaming platform headquartered in Austin, Texas, must remain completely stateless while still preserving user session state, such as playback queues and authentication tokens.

How can the session state data be maintained externally while keeping latency at the LOWEST possible value?

Your answer is correct
Create an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the cluster for session data storage

Explanation

Correct. Amazon ElastiCache for Redis is an in-memory data store. An in-memory data store delivers the lowest possible latency for reading and writing session state data. This latency is lower than disk-based or query-engine-based alternatives. Keyword tip: When a scenario emphasizes the lowest latency for session or cache data, ElastiCache for Redis or Memcached is almost always the correct choice, because of its in-memory architecture.
Create an Amazon Redshift instance, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage a database inside the Redshift cluster for session data storage

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse service. Amazon Redshift is designed for OLAP workloads, such as large-scale analytics and business intelligence queries. Amazon Redshift is not built for low-latency transactional storage of session state data. Keyword tip: If a scenario pairs Redshift with a real-time application need, treat it as a distractor, because Redshift's query engine optimizes for complex analytical queries, not fast key-based lookups.
Create an Amazon DynamoDB table, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the table for session data storage

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon DynamoDB is a strong option for storing session state externally. Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed key-value store with single-digit millisecond latency. However, Amazon DynamoDB still involves persistent storage and network round trips. These round trips make Amazon DynamoDB slightly slower than an in-memory solution like Amazon ElastiCache. Keyword tip: When a question asks specifically for the absolute lowest latency rather than just a scalable or durable solution, choose ElastiCache over DynamoDB.
Implement a shared Amazon EFS file system solution across the underlying Amazon EC2 instances, then implement session handling at the application level to leverage the EFS file system for session data storage

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EFS can be shared across multiple Amazon EC2 instances. Amazon EFS could technically store session files. However, a file-system-based approach adds higher latency than a purpose-built key-value store. This approach also adds unnecessary complexity for simple session read and write operations. Keyword tip: Amazon EFS is best suited for shared file storage and content management, not for high-throughput, low-latency session or key-value data.

This question tests the ability to externalize session state for a stateless web tier while minimizing latency. This pattern is common in horizontally scalable, fault-tolerant three-tier architectures. Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon ElastiCache are both valid key-value stores for session data. Amazon ElastiCache's in-memory architecture gives Amazon ElastiCache a decisive latency advantage over disk-backed or query-engine services like Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon EFS. The correct decision process is to first eliminate options unsuited to key-value access patterns, such as Amazon Redshift for analytics and Amazon EFS for file storage, then choose between the remaining key-value stores based on whether the requirement is durability and scalability, which favors Amazon DynamoDB, or the lowest possible latency, which favors Amazon ElastiCache.

Consider this scenario: Saltmarsh Holdings needs to serve a sudden spike in concurrent listeners without slowing down song playback or authentication checks. By storing session data, such as playback queue and login state, in Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, Saltmarsh Holdings keeps each user's session lookup in-memory. This approach avoids added latency during peak streaming hours. This design lets the web tier scale out horizontally without losing track of individual listener sessions.

Question 27Incorrect

Storing files that are accessed infrequently but must remain concurrently accessible by hundreds of Amazon EC2 instances requires a storage service that balances low cost with immediate data availability. Anchor Logistics, a maritime shipping company that tracks vessel manifests and cargo documentation across its fleet, needs the most cost-effective file storage service that still provides immediate access to the data whenever it is needed.

Which of the following options represents the best solution for these requirements?

Correct answer
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) Standard-IA storage class

Explanation

Correct. Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic file storage service. Amazon EFS provides a standard file system interface with strong consistency and file locking, and thousands of EC2 instances can access the same file system at the same time. The EFS Standard-IA storage class lowers storage cost for files that are not accessed every day, while still giving immediate, millisecond-latency access when the data is needed. Keyword tip: the phrase "infrequently accessed but instantly available shared file system for many EC2 instances" points to EFS Standard-IA.
Your answer is incorrect
Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) Standard storage class

Explanation

Incorrect. The EFS Standard storage class is optimized for files that are accessed frequently. EFS Standard costs more than EFS Standard-IA, so EFS Standard does not meet the requirement to minimize cost for infrequently accessed data. Keyword tip: when the scenario emphasizes "less frequently accessed" together with "cost-effective," choose the IA storage class instead of the Standard tier.
Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS)

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon EBS is a block-level storage service. In almost all configurations, EBS attaches to only one EC2 instance at a time; EBS Multi-Attach is limited to specific Nitro-based instance types and io1/io2 volumes, and it does not provide a file system. Amazon EBS cannot serve as a shared file store for hundreds of concurrent EC2 instances. Keyword tip: EBS is single-instance block storage, not a concurrently shared file store.
Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Applications access S3 through an internet API, not through a file system interface. Amazon S3 does not provide the POSIX-compliant file system that hundreds of EC2 instances need for concurrent shared access. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires a shared file system interface instead of API-based object access, rule out S3 storage classes.

This question tests the ability to match an AWS storage service and storage class to an access pattern, a concurrency requirement, and a cost goal. Use Amazon S3 when the application accesses data as objects through an API. Use Amazon EBS when a single EC2 instance needs block storage. Use Amazon EFS when many EC2 instances need a shared, POSIX-compliant file system at the same time. Within EFS, choose the Standard-IA storage class when the files are accessed infrequently, because Standard-IA lowers storage cost while still giving immediate access and the same durability as EFS Standard.

Real-world example: Anchor Logistics stores historical vessel manifests and customs documents that hundreds of EC2 instances in its fleet-tracking application must read on demand, but most of these files are opened only a few times per month after the shipment closes. Placing these files on EFS Standard-IA lets every instance mount the same file system and read a manifest immediately when a port inspector or customs officer requests it, while Anchor Logistics avoids paying the higher EFS Standard rate for data that sits idle most of the time.

Question 28Incorrect

A team of developers at Driftline Analytics currently builds, bundles, and packages its network-monitoring software using a third-party tool that runs entirely on-premises, and the resulting package is stored on a local file system. As Driftline Analytics, a telecommunications provider, expands the fleet of Amazon EC2 instances that process call detail records, the team must now deploy this on-premises software package onto those EC2 instances.

How can the application be deployed onto the EC2 instances?

Your answer is incorrect
Create a repository using AWS CodeCommit to automatically trigger a deployment to the EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeCommit is a managed source control service based on Git. AWS CodeCommit stores and versions source code, not pre-built packages created by an external tool. In this scenario, the package was already built and packaged outside AWS, so there is no source code for CodeCommit to store. AWS CodeCommit also does not natively trigger deployments to EC2 instances. Keyword tip: CodeCommit is a version control repository, not a deployment mechanism.
Use AWS CodeBuild to commit the package and automatically deploy the software package

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed build service. AWS CodeBuild compiles source code, runs tests, and produces deployable artifacts. AWS CodeBuild does not commit packages to a repository, and AWS CodeBuild does not deploy packages to EC2 instances. Keyword tip: if a scenario describes compiling, testing, or building artifacts, think CodeBuild. If a scenario describes deploying a package to compute targets, think CodeDeploy instead.
Use AWS CodeDeploy and point it to the local file system to deploy the software package

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy cannot read a deployment package directly from an on-premises local file system. AWS CodeDeploy requires the deployment revision to be stored in one of two locations: an Amazon S3 bucket or a GitHub repository. Keyword tip: when a question describes an on-premises build artifact that needs deployment, remember that CodeDeploy needs the package staged in S3 or GitHub first.
Correct answer
Upload the bundle to an Amazon S3 bucket and specify the S3 location when performing a deployment using AWS CodeDeploy

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodeDeploy supports deploying application revisions that have been uploaded as an archive, commonly a .zip file, to an Amazon S3 bucket. The developer specifies the S3 bucket and object location as the deployment source. AWS CodeDeploy then retrieves the archive from S3 and deploys it to the target EC2 instances. Keyword tip: the pattern "upload to S3, then deploy with CodeDeploy" is the standard approach for deploying externally built packages to EC2 instances.

This question tests knowledge of how AWS CodeDeploy sources deployment artifacts when the build process happens outside of AWS. AWS CodeDeploy supports exactly two revision sources: an Amazon S3 bucket, where the package is stored as a compressed archive, or a GitHub repository. AWS CodeDeploy cannot read a package directly from an on-premises or local file system. AWS CodeBuild is used for building and testing code, and AWS CodeCommit is used for source control; neither of these services deploys artifacts to EC2 instances. The correct workflow is to upload the packaged software to Amazon S3 first, and then reference that S3 location when creating an AWS CodeDeploy deployment that targets the EC2 instances.

Consider this scenario: Driftline Analytics builds its call-detail-record processing software using an on-premises third-party packaging tool, so the resulting archive exists only on a local file system. Before the operations team can deploy this archive to the EC2 fleet, they must first upload it to an Amazon S3 bucket that AWS CodeDeploy can access. Once the archive is in S3, the team creates a CodeDeploy deployment that points to that S3 object, and CodeDeploy handles pulling the package onto each EC2 instance and running the deployment lifecycle hooks.

Question 29Correct

Calling an HTTP API endpoint that a partner operates requires embedding an existing API key into a backend service without adding any noticeable latency to that service. Lumen Cooperative, an e-learning platform headquartered in Austin, Texas, needs to share learner analytics data with this partner endpoint and already holds the required API key.

What is the most secure approach for storing and retrieving the API key at runtime?

Keep the API key in an encrypted file in Amazon S3, and fetch the API key from S3 at runtime by using the AWS SDK to make the API call

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing the API key in an encrypted file in Amazon S3 still requires the application to handle encryption, decryption, and key rotation manually. Amazon S3 is a general-purpose object storage service, not a secrets-management service, so it lacks built-in secret rotation. Keyword tip: treat any option that stores secrets in S3, EBS, or a flat file as a red flag for secure secret storage.
Your answer is correct
Keep the API key in AWS Secrets Manager, and fetch the API key at runtime by using the AWS SDK to make the API call

Explanation

Correct. AWS Secrets Manager is designed to store, retrieve, and automatically rotate secrets such as API keys. The application retrieves the API key at runtime through the AWS SDK, so the API key never appears in source code or a database table. AWS Secrets Manager also supports a client-side caching library, which stores the API key locally after the first retrieval and avoids repeated calls to Secrets Manager on every request. This caching behavior satisfies the requirement to avoid a negative performance impact. Keyword tip: look for scenario clues that combine secure storage, automatic rotation, and a need to avoid added latency — these clues point to AWS Secrets Manager with client-side caching.
Keep the API key in a local code variable, and use the local code variable at runtime to make the API call

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing the API key in a local code variable means the API key is embedded directly in the source code. Anyone with access to the code repository or version control history can read the API key. Changing the API key later requires a code change and a new deployment. Keyword tip: any option that describes a credential hardcoded in application code is almost always the wrong answer on this exam.
Keep the API key in an encrypted table in Amazon RDS for MySQL, and fetch the API key from RDS at runtime by using the AWS SDK to make the API call

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing the API key in an encrypted Amazon RDS for MySQL table requires the application to manage database connections and access controls. The application team must also build manual rotation logic, because RDS does not rotate secrets automatically. This approach adds operational overhead and does not meet the requirement for a low-maintenance, secure storage solution. Keyword tip: watch for options that use a general-purpose database as a credential store instead of a dedicated secrets service.

AWS Secrets Manager is the AWS service built specifically for storing, retrieving, and automatically rotating secrets such as API keys and database credentials. Storing a secret in a database table, an S3 object, or a hardcoded code variable each requires the application team to build custom logic for rotation, access control, and secure retrieval, because none of those services provide this natively. AWS Secrets Manager removes this operational burden and adds audit logging plus IAM-based access control on top of automatic rotation for supported services. To avoid a performance hit at runtime, Secrets Manager works with a client-side caching library, so the application fetches the secret once and reuses the cached value for later calls instead of calling Secrets Manager on every request.

Real-world example: Lumen Cooperative's course-recommendation service calls a third-party analytics API to enrich learner profiles, and the API key for that call is stored in AWS Secrets Manager. The application uses the AWS Secrets Manager caching client to retrieve the API key once and cache it locally, so thousands of course page loads per minute do not each trigger a separate Secrets Manager call. This design keeps the API key out of source code and application logs while meeting the platform's low-latency requirement.

Question 30Incorrect

Juniper Council needs to determine why a newly deployed AWS Lambda function is not producing any log entries in Amazon CloudWatch Logs, even though the function completes successfully every time it runs. Juniper Council is a video conferencing SaaS company that recently migrated a notification microservice to a serverless architecture.

A developer manually invoked the function several times through the AWS CLI, and each invocation returned a success message, but after waiting 15 minutes, still no log data appears in CloudWatch Logs.

What is the most likely explanation for this issue?

The function configuration does not have CloudWatch Logs configured as a success destination.

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda Destinations apply only to asynchronous invocations. A destination routes the invocation result, either success or failure, to a target such as an SNS topic, an SQS queue, EventBridge, or another Lambda function. CloudWatch Logs is not a valid destination type. Destinations do not control whether execution logs appear in CloudWatch Logs. Keyword tip: if a question describes routing invocation results to another service, think Destinations; if a question describes missing execution logs, think IAM permissions instead.
The Lambda function does not have any explicit log statements to send log data to CloudWatch Logs.

Explanation

Incorrect. A function needs explicit logging statements to produce custom log content. This fact does not explain a complete absence of log data. Lambda always writes platform-generated log lines for every invocation: START, END, and REPORT. These platform log lines appear even when the function code contains no logging statements at all. A complete absence of any log data, including these platform lines, points to a permissions problem, not missing log statements. Keyword tip: platform log lines (START, END, REPORT) always appear when permissions are correct, even without custom logging code.
Your answer is incorrect
A log group and log stream have not been configured for the function in CloudWatch Logs.

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda automatically creates the log group and log stream for a function. Lambda names the log group /aws/lambda/<function-name>. Lambda creates these resources the first time the function successfully writes a log entry, as long as the execution role has the needed permissions. The developer does not need to create the log group or log stream manually. Keyword tip: automatic log group and log stream creation is default Lambda behavior, so their absence is not the root cause unless permissions are also missing.
Correct answer
The function execution role does not have permission to write log data to CloudWatch Logs.

Explanation

Correct. The Lambda execution role must include permissions for three CloudWatch Logs actions: logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents. The function needs these permissions to publish any log data, including the automatic START, END, and REPORT entries. If the execution role is missing these permissions, the function still runs and returns a success message. However, Lambda silently fails to create the log group and log stream, and no log events get written, so no log output appears no matter how long you wait. Keyword tip: a successful invocation with zero log output after several minutes is the classic sign of a missing or misconfigured execution role IAM policy for CloudWatch Logs.

This scenario tests understanding of how AWS Lambda integrates with Amazon CloudWatch Logs, and the role that IAM permissions play in that integration. Lambda automatically creates a log group and log stream, and Lambda writes both platform-generated entries (START, END, REPORT) and any custom log statements, but only if the function's execution role grants the required logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents permissions. When a function executes successfully but produces no log output at all after a reasonable wait, the most likely cause is a missing or misconfigured execution role policy. Missing log statements, missing destinations, and missing log group or stream configuration are not the cause, because Lambda either handles those automatically or they are unrelated to logging delivery.

Applied example: Juniper Council's developer team deployed a Lambda-based notification microservice for its video conferencing platform and needed to confirm that meeting-alert events were processing correctly. When CloudWatch Logs showed no entries despite successful CLI test invocations, the team checked the function's execution role first, and found that the role was missing the logs:PutLogEvents permission, which they corrected by attaching the AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole managed policy.

Question 31Correct

Copperfield Robotics runs a serverless web application for its property and casualty insurance platform, using AWS Lambda functions integrated with a REST API deployed through Amazon API Gateway. The development team maintains multiple code branches, and the company now wants to avoid updating the API Gateway target endpoint every time a new code push is performed.

What solution would allow the developer to update the Lambda code without needing to update the REST API configuration?

Your answer is correct
Create aliases and versions in AWS Lambda.

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda alias acts as a pointer to a specific function version. Each alias has its own stable Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The developer configures the REST API integration to invoke the function through the alias ARN. After that setup, the developer can publish new function versions and repoint the alias to them. The API Gateway integration target never needs to change. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for a stable invocation target that survives Lambda code updates, think of aliases and versions.
Create multiple stages and deployments.

Explanation

Incorrect. API Gateway stages and deployments control which snapshot of the API configuration is exposed at a given URL path. This configuration includes resources, methods, and stage variables. Stages and deployments do not by themselves separate the integration from a specific Lambda function ARN. Without a Lambda alias, each new function version still requires updating the stage's integration target. Keyword tip: stages manage API deployment snapshots, not Lambda version pointers, unless the stage also uses stage variables that reference an alias.
Create multiple private API endpoints and use CNAMEs.

Explanation

Incorrect. Creating multiple private API endpoints produces separate, isolated APIs instead of a single API that can point to different Lambda code versions. This approach adds unnecessary complexity. It does not solve the problem of separating the API configuration from the underlying function code. Keyword tip: private endpoints and CNAMEs relate to network isolation and custom domain routing. They do not relate to code versioning.
Create different tags for each Lambda function.

Explanation

Incorrect. Tags on a Lambda function are key-value metadata. Tags are used for cost allocation, resource organization, and access control policies. Tags have no functional role in defining or resolving the integration endpoint that API Gateway invokes. Keyword tip: if an option mentions tags for routing or invocation purposes, treat it as a distractor, because tags are purely informational.

This question tests understanding of AWS Lambda aliases and versions as a mechanism to separate a stable invocation endpoint from the underlying function code that changes with each deployment. A Lambda version is an immutable snapshot of function code. A Lambda alias is a mutable pointer to a specific version. When API Gateway invokes the function through the alias ARN, API Gateway always calls a fixed ARN, even while the alias is repointed to new versions during deployments. Stages, tags, and private endpoints solve different problems: stages manage API configuration snapshots, tags manage metadata, and private endpoints manage network isolation, so none of them remove the need to update the integration target when the function code changes.

Consider this scenario: Copperfield Robotics deploys a claims-processing Lambda function behind a REST API used by its insurance agents. The development team creates a "PROD" alias pointing to the current stable version. When the team publishes a new version after a code push, it repoints the PROD alias to the new version instead of editing the API Gateway integration. Agents keep using the same API endpoint without interruption, and the team can also shift a small percentage of traffic to the new version for a canary test before fully repointing the alias.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-aliases.html

Deployment
Question 32Incorrect

Kingsford Robotics needs to fix a bug that blocks brand-new users from accessing its public API immediately after they self-register, a state government agency that issues permits for autonomous robotics operations. The agency maintains a REST API service using Amazon API Gateway with native API key validation.

A new self-service registration portal creates an API key for each signup by calling CreateApiKey and emails the key to the user. When a newly registered user calls the API with this key, the request fails with a 403 Forbidden error, while existing users continue to call the API without any issue.

What code update will grant these new users access to the API?

Your answer is incorrect
The updateAuthorizer method must be called to update the API's authorizer to include the newly created API key

Explanation

Incorrect. The updateAuthorizer method changes settings on a Lambda or Amazon Cognito authorizer. An authorizer handles token-based or custom authorization, which is a separate mechanism from native API key validation. Updating an authorizer has no effect on API keys or usage plans. Keyword tip: authorizer methods apply to custom, Lambda, or Cognito-based access control, not to the built-in API key and usage plan mechanism described in this scenario.
Correct answer
The createUsagePlanKey method must be called to associate the newly created API key with the correct usage plan

Explanation

Correct. A usage plan controls which API keys can access deployed API stages and methods. A usage plan also enforces throttling and quota limits for each key. A newly created API key has no usage plan attached to it by default. API Gateway rejects requests from a key with no usage plan, even if the key itself is valid. The agency's code must call createUsagePlanKey to link the new key to the correct usage plan before the key can be used. Keyword tip: when a new API key returns a 403 error but older keys still work, suspect a missing usage plan link and look for createUsagePlanKey.
The createDeployment method must be called so the API can be redeployed to include the newly created API key

Explanation

Incorrect. Calling createDeployment pushes configuration changes, such as new resources or methods, to an API stage. A new deployment does not create or change any link between an API key and a usage plan. Keyword tip: deployments affect stage configuration only, they do not affect API key-to-usage-plan relationships.
The importApiKeys method must be called to import all newly created API keys into the current stage of the API

Explanation

Incorrect. The importApiKeys method loads many API keys into API Gateway at once from an external source, such as a CSV file. This method is not used for keys that a program already created one at a time through CreateApiKey. Keyword tip: importApiKeys applies to bulk import of externally generated keys, not to linking one existing key to a usage plan.

This question tests how Amazon API Gateway's native API key validation works together with usage plans. Creating an API key with CreateApiKey only generates the key value. The key grants no access on its own. A separate call to createUsagePlanKey is required to attach the key to a usage plan, and that usage plan defines which stages and methods the key can reach, along with its throttling and quota limits. The other options fail for distinct reasons: importApiKeys only bulk-loads externally generated keys, createDeployment only updates stage configuration, and updateAuthorizer only manages Lambda or Cognito authorizers, none of which touch the API key-to-usage-plan link. When new keys fail with a 403 error while old keys keep working, trace the request flow and check for a missing usage plan association before suspecting a deployment or authorizer problem.

Real-world example: A state government agency like Kingsford Robotics often launches self-service portals so citizens or partner companies can register for API access without manual approval. If the registration code only calls CreateApiKey and skips createUsagePlanKey, every new signup receives a key that looks valid but is rejected by API Gateway, while staff who set up accounts manually months earlier remain unaffected because their keys were already linked to a usage plan.

Question 33Correct

A recent internal audit found that application log data for a containerized workload was scattered across ephemeral compute resources with no centralized retention, creating a compliance gap. The workload belongs to Larkspur Alliance, a supply chain visibility startup that runs its application on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) using the AWS Fargate launch type.

To satisfy the audit finding, all application log data must be logged and stored centrally on AWS.

How should this requirement be configured?

Your answer is correct
Use the awslogs log driver to configure the containers in your tasks to send log information to CloudWatch Logs. Add the required logConfiguration parameters to your task definition

Explanation

Correct. The awslogs log driver lets you configure the containers in an ECS task to send log output directly to CloudWatch Logs. For tasks running on the Fargate launch type, you must add the logConfiguration parameters to the task definition. These parameters include the log driver name, log group, region, and stream prefix. This configuration is required because Fargate does not give you access to an underlying EC2 instance to manage. Keyword tip: when a Fargate-based ECS scenario asks for centralized application log collection, the correct pattern is the awslogs log driver plus logConfiguration in the task definition.
Use the awslogs log driver to send log information to CloudWatch Logs. To turn on the awslogs log driver, your Amazon ECS container instances require at least version 1.9.0 of the container agent

Explanation

Incorrect. This statement describes a real ECS requirement, but it applies to the EC2 launch type. ECS container instances running on EC2 need container agent version 1.9.0 or later to support the awslogs log driver. In this scenario, the launch type is Fargate. Fargate has no container agent version to manage, because AWS manages the underlying infrastructure. Keyword tip: container agent version requirements point to the EC2 launch type, not to Fargate.
Amazon ECS metric data is automatically sent to CloudWatch in 1-minute periods. An Amazon ECS service using the Fargate launch type has CloudWatch CPU and memory utilization metrics that can be enabled from the ECS console

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon ECS does automatically send CPU and memory utilization metrics to CloudWatch every minute for Fargate services, with no manual configuration needed. However, these are infrastructure performance metrics, not application log data. The audit requirement in this scenario asks for centralized application log content, which requires the awslogs log driver. Built-in resource metrics do not satisfy this requirement. Keyword tip: separate CloudWatch metrics, which track resource utilization, from CloudWatch Logs, which stores application log content.
Download and install the unified CloudWatch agent on the ECS instances to collect internal system-level metrics and application logs from the instances. The logs collected by the unified CloudWatch agent are processed and stored in Amazon CloudWatch Logs and can be queried for report generation

Explanation

Incorrect. The unified CloudWatch agent must be installed on a compute instance that you manage. Fargate does not expose an underlying instance for software installation, so this approach is not possible. The unified CloudWatch agent approach applies only to ECS tasks running on the EC2 launch type, where you control the instance. Keyword tip: any answer that describes installing an agent on ECS instances signals an EC2 launch type solution, not a Fargate solution.

This question tests the ability to centralize application logs for a containerized workload running on Amazon ECS with the AWS Fargate launch type, where there is no direct access to the underlying instance. The awslogs log driver, configured through the logConfiguration parameters in the task definition, is the standard mechanism to stream container application logs to CloudWatch Logs for centralized storage and querying. The unified CloudWatch agent and container agent version requirements apply only to the EC2 launch type, and built-in CloudWatch metrics cover resource utilization, not application log content. When designing a logging solution for ECS, match the launch type, either EC2 or Fargate, to the logging mechanism that launch type actually supports.

Applied example: Larkspur Alliance, a supply chain visibility startup, runs its shipment-tracking API on ECS Fargate tasks. After an audit flags missing centralized log retention, the engineering team updates the task definition to use the awslogs log driver with a dedicated CloudWatch Logs group, so every container's output is captured and searchable in one place for future audits.

Question 34Incorrect

Northbridge Solutions, a water utility company, needs a bucket policy that denies the upload object permission for any request that does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header requesting server-side encryption with SSE-KMS, because the Amazon S3 bucket named northbridge-meter-readings stores sensitive meter-reading data subject to critical-infrastructure data protection requirements.

Which of the following policies is the right fit for this requirement?

Your answer is incorrect
{ "Version":"2012-10-17", "Id":"PutObjectPolicy", "Statement":[{ "Sid":"DenyUnEncryptedObjectUploads", "Effect":"Deny", "Principal":"*", "Action":"s3:GetObject", "Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::northbridge-meter-readings/*", "Condition":{ "StringNotEquals":{ "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"aws:AES256" } } } ] }

Explanation

Incorrect. This policy targets the s3:GetObject action instead of the s3:PutObject action. The s3:GetObject action controls read access, not the encryption used during object uploads. This policy also checks for the value aws:AES256. The value aws:AES256 corresponds to SSE-S3 (server-side encryption with Amazon S3-managed keys), not SSE-KMS. The requirement calls for enforcing SSE-KMS on uploads. Both the action and the condition value in this policy are wrong for that requirement. Keyword tip: s3:GetObject controls read access, while s3:PutObject controls upload access; AES256 signals SSE-S3, while aws:kms signals SSE-KMS.
Correct answer
{ "Version":"2012-10-17", "Id":"PutObjectPolicy", "Statement":[{ "Sid":"DenyUnEncryptedObjectUploads", "Effect":"Deny", "Principal":"*", "Action":"s3:PutObject", "Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::northbridge-meter-readings/*", "Condition":{ "StringNotEquals":{ "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"aws:kms" } } } ] }

Explanation

Correct. This bucket policy denies the s3:PutObject action whenever the request does not include the x-amz-server-side-encryption header set to aws:kms. The policy uses the StringNotEquals condition operator to check this. This design forces every object upload to the bucket to use SSE-KMS encryption. Any request that lacks the required header value gets denied. Keyword tip: to enforce a required condition on all requests, pair Effect: Deny with StringNotEquals on the required value, so anything other than that value gets blocked.
{ "Version":"2012-10-17", "Id":"PutObjectPolicy", "Statement":[{ "Sid":"DenyUnEncryptedObjectUploads", "Effect":"Deny", "Principal":"*", "Action":"s3:PutObject", "Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::northbridge-meter-readings/*", "Condition":{ "StringNotEquals":{ "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"false" } } } ] }

Explanation

Incorrect. This policy checks the header value against the literal string "false". The string "false" is not a valid server-side encryption algorithm identifier. This condition would never match legitimate requests correctly, so the policy logic does not enforce encryption. The condition value must be a valid encryption algorithm identifier, such as aws:kms for SSE-KMS or AES256 for SSE-S3. Keyword tip: the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption condition key only accepts valid encryption algorithm values like aws:kms or AES256, never boolean-like strings.
{ "Version":"2012-10-17", "Id":"PutObjectPolicy", "Statement":[{ "Sid":"DenyUnEncryptedObjectUploads", "Effect":"Deny", "Principal":"*", "Action":"s3:PutObject", "Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::northbridge-meter-readings/*", "Condition":{ "StringEquals":{ "s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption":"aws:kms" } } } ] }

Explanation

Incorrect. This policy uses the StringEquals operator. The StringEquals operator denies the s3:PutObject action only when the request DOES include the aws:kms encryption header. This behavior is the opposite of what the policy needs. The policy must deny uploads that lack the required encryption header. To do that, the condition operator must be StringNotEquals. Keyword tip: when a policy must block requests that are missing a specific header value, look for StringNotEquals, not StringEquals.

This question tests the ability to construct an Amazon S3 bucket policy condition that enforces server-side encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS) on all uploaded objects. The correct approach combines Effect: Deny, the s3:PutObject action, and a StringNotEquals condition on the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption key set to aws:kms. This combination denies any upload request that does not explicitly request SSE-KMS encryption. Use StringEquals when a policy needs to match a specific value directly. Use StringNotEquals when a policy needs to deny everything except one specific required value. Also distinguish AES256 (SSE-S3) from aws:kms (SSE-KMS), since these values represent different encryption mechanisms, and remember that s3:GetObject governs read access while s3:PutObject governs write access. To require one specific AWS KMS key rather than any SSE-KMS key, a policy can additionally use the s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption-aws-kms-key-id condition key with the key's ARN.

Real-world example: Northbridge Solutions stores sensitive meter-reading data in Amazon S3 as part of its water utility operations. Regulatory requirements for critical infrastructure data mandate that this data stay encrypted at rest with an AWS KMS key. Northbridge Solutions applies a bucket policy like the one described here to reject any upload request that does not specify SSE-KMS encryption, so no application or user can accidentally store unencrypted meter data in the bucket.

Question 35Incorrect

Yellowpine Foundation, a healthcare diagnostics provider, runs its diagnostic imaging processing pipeline on Amazon EC2 instances inside an Auto Scaling group. The group currently scales only on the default CPU utilization metric.

Because imaging workloads consume far more memory than CPU, the engineering team now needs the group to scale based on average RAM usage across the fleet's instances.

Which option provides the best solution?

Migrate the application to AWS Lambda

Explanation

Incorrect. Migrating the application to AWS Lambda does not solve the stated problem. The requirement is to scale an existing Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances based on RAM usage. Moving to Lambda changes the entire compute model and removes the Auto Scaling group altogether, so it does not meet the requirement. Keyword tip: when a scenario explicitly requires Auto Scaling group behavior, discard any option that proposes migrating to a different, unrelated compute service.
Create a custom alarm for the Auto Scaling group and make the instances trigger the alarm using a PutAlarmData API

Explanation

Incorrect. There is no AWS API named PutAlarmData. CloudWatch alarms are created from metric data. Instances do not trigger alarms directly. Even if such an API existed, a single instance cannot know the average RAM usage across the whole fleet on its own. Yellowpine Foundation needs a shared custom metric that aggregates data from all instances, which only the CloudWatch custom metric approach provides. Keyword tip: watch for invented or nonexistent API names in answer choices. This is a common sign of an incorrect distractor.
Your answer is incorrect
Enable detailed monitoring for EC2 and the Auto Scaling group to get the RAM usage data and create a CloudWatch alarm on top of it

Explanation

Incorrect. Detailed monitoring changes only the frequency of standard Amazon EC2 metrics. Detailed monitoring sends these standard metrics every 1 minute instead of every 5 minutes. Detailed monitoring does not add new metrics. Memory utilization is not a standard metric that Amazon EC2 publishes, because the hypervisor cannot see inside the operating system. Yellowpine Foundation would still need to create and push a custom metric to track RAM usage. Keyword tip: 'detailed monitoring' only changes how often existing standard metrics are reported. It does not create new metrics like RAM usage.
Correct answer
Create a custom metric in CloudWatch and make the instances send data to it using PutMetricData. Then, create an alarm based on this metric

Explanation

Correct. Amazon CloudWatch does not collect memory usage for Amazon EC2 instances by default. RAM usage is internal to the operating system, so the hypervisor cannot report it automatically. To track RAM usage, Yellowpine Foundation must install an agent or script on each instance. That agent calls the PutMetricData API to publish RAM usage as a custom metric to CloudWatch. Yellowpine Foundation then creates a CloudWatch alarm based on this custom metric, and the Auto Scaling group's scaling policy uses that alarm to trigger scaling actions. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks to scale on a metric that Amazon EC2 does not report by default, such as RAM, disk usage, or a custom application metric, think 'custom metric plus PutMetricData'.

This question tests understanding of Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics and how they connect to Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling policies when the desired scaling metric is not collected by AWS automatically. Memory utilization is not a standard Amazon EC2 metric, because the hypervisor cannot see inside the guest operating system. The correct approach is to publish RAM usage as a custom metric using the PutMetricData API, often through the CloudWatch agent installed on each instance, and then create a CloudWatch alarm on that custom metric to drive the Auto Scaling group's scaling policy. Detailed monitoring only increases the reporting frequency of existing standard metrics, and it never creates new ones, while unrelated compute migrations or nonexistent APIs serve only as distractors.

In practice: Yellowpine Foundation's diagnostic imaging pipeline processes large image files that consume significant memory during analysis, so CPU utilization alone does not reflect real workload pressure on the fleet. By installing the CloudWatch agent on each Amazon EC2 instance and publishing memory utilization as a custom metric, Yellowpine Foundation can create a CloudWatch alarm that triggers the Auto Scaling group to add instances precisely when RAM pressure rises, keeping diagnostic turnaround times consistent for clinicians awaiting results.

Question 36Incorrect

A newly published research report on citywide traffic sensor performance contains sensitive findings that must be shared with a distributed team of urban planning consultants working from multiple countries. Cobalt National, a smart city government agency, hosts its public data portal on Amazon EC2 instances behind Amazon CloudFront and needs to grant access to this single document without weakening the security posture of the distribution.

Which of the following represents the most optimal solution to address this requirement without compromising the security of the content?

Use the CloudFront signed cookies feature to control access to the file

Explanation

Incorrect. Signed cookies work best when a team needs access to multiple restricted files, such as an entire subscriber area, without changing existing URLs. A signed cookie applies broadly across many files at once. For a single file, using a signed cookie adds unnecessary complexity, and if a signed URL and a signed cookie both apply to the same file, CloudFront gives priority to the signed URL. Keyword tip: signed cookies fit multi-file access without changing URLs; signed URLs fit single-file, fine-grained access.
Your answer is incorrect
Configure AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) to monitor and control the HTTP and HTTPS requests that are forwarded to CloudFront

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS WAF monitors and filters HTTP and HTTPS requests forwarded to CloudFront based on rules such as IP address ranges or query string values. AWS WAF is designed for broader application-layer protection, such as blocking malicious traffic patterns. AWS WAF does not grant time-limited access to a specific file for legitimate users. Keyword tip: AWS WAF filters or blocks malicious traffic; AWS WAF does not distribute controlled access to content.
Correct answer
Use the CloudFront signed URL feature to control access to the file

Explanation

Correct. A CloudFront signed URL attaches an expiration time and access conditions directly to the URL used to retrieve one specific file. A signed URL gives precise, per-object control over who can download the file and for how long. A signed URL is the most efficient and secure way to share one restricted document with a distributed team without changing broader access policies. Keyword tip: a single restricted file with time-limited or conditional access points to a signed URL.
Use CloudFront's Field-Level Encryption to help protect sensitive data

Explanation

Incorrect. CloudFront field-level encryption encrypts specific sensitive fields inside an HTTPS POST request, such as form data, before that data reaches the origin server. Field-level encryption uses field-specific keys to protect the data while it travels through intermediate systems. Field-level encryption does not control who can download or view a distributed file, so field-level encryption does not meet the requirement of restricting access to a single research report. Keyword tip: field-level encryption protects POST form data fields, not file downloads.

This question tests knowledge of CloudFront's private content distribution mechanisms. A signed URL restricts access to a single file and includes an expiration time directly in the URL, which makes it ideal when only one object needs controlled, time-limited access. A signed cookie restricts access to multiple files at once without requiring changes to each URL, which makes it better suited for broader content areas. Field-level encryption protects specific form data fields in transit to the origin, and AWS WAF filters incoming requests for malicious traffic patterns; neither of these two options controls which legitimate users can download a specific file, so the decision comes down to matching the scope of the requirement, one file versus many, with the correct access-control feature.

Practical example: Cobalt National, a smart city government agency, could use a CloudFront signed URL to share a single traffic sensor research report with an external consulting team. The agency generates a signed URL with a short expiration window, sends the URL to the consultants, and the URL stops working automatically once the review period ends, without granting the consultants any broader access to the agency's public data portal.

Question 37Correct

Following a security audit that flagged unencrypted message queues as a compliance risk, stricter data-protection requirements were introduced for applications running in AWS GovCloud (US). Thornfield Holdings, a theme park operator that manages ticketing and ride-reservation systems under a government contract, relies on Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) as the message queue service for these applications.

As the contract developer supporting Thornfield Holdings, you must ensure the queue data is encrypted at rest.

Which of the following steps can you take to meet this requirement without making any changes to the existing application code?

Use AWS Secrets Manager

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Secrets Manager stores, rotates, and retrieves secrets such as database credentials and API keys. AWS Secrets Manager does not encrypt message data stored inside an SQS queue. Using AWS Secrets Manager would not satisfy the stated requirement, because it solves a different problem than queue encryption. Keyword tip: Secrets Manager manages credentials and secrets. It does not encrypt message payloads in a queue.
Use the SSL endpoint

Explanation

Incorrect. The SSL endpoint protects data only while it moves between the client and the SQS service. This protection is called encryption in transit. The SSL endpoint does not encrypt the message data while it sits in the queue. The requirement asks for encrypted queues, which means encryption at rest. Encryption at rest is a different protection than encryption in transit. Keyword tip: SSL/TLS endpoints protect data in transit. They do not protect stored data.
Your answer is correct
Enable SQS KMS encryption

Explanation

Correct. Enabling SQS server-side encryption (SSE) with AWS KMS lets Amazon SQS automatically encrypt message bodies as they are stored. This encryption applies to both Standard and FIFO queues. AWS KMS manages the encryption keys used for this process. You enable this feature through a queue configuration setting, not through application code. Keyword tip: SQS SSE with AWS KMS is a configuration-only setting that adds encryption at rest without touching application code.
Use client-side encryption

Explanation

Incorrect. Client-side encryption means the application encrypts the message before sending it to the queue. The application must also decrypt the message after retrieving it. Building this encryption and decryption logic requires changes to the existing application code. The question states that no code changes are allowed, so client-side encryption does not meet the requirement. Keyword tip: client-side encryption always requires code changes in the application.

This question tests the difference between encryption in transit and encryption at rest, and the difference between configuration-based and code-based solutions. Use the SSL/TLS endpoint to protect data while it travels between the client and SQS. Use client-side encryption only when the application must control the encryption keys and process itself, since this approach always requires code changes. Use SQS server-side encryption (SSE) with AWS KMS when the requirement is encryption at rest with no code changes, because this feature is enabled through queue configuration alone. The decision logic requires identifying that the requirement is about stored data, not transmitted data, and that the solution must not touch the application code.

Use case: A theme park operator like Thornfield Holdings often processes ticketing and ride-reservation messages through SQS queues that carry visitor payment references and reservation details. After a security audit flags these queues as a compliance gap, the fastest and safest fix is to enable SQS server-side encryption with AWS KMS on the affected queues, since this closes the gap immediately without requiring the ticketing application to be redeployed or modified.
