Question 38Incorrect

Bluecrest Foundation needs to optimize a CPU-bound AWS Lambda function that computes diagnostic imaging results, so it can guarantee fast response times for time-critical patient reports. As a healthcare diagnostics provider processing urgent test results, Bluecrest Foundation requires the function to finish its calculations quickly.

What action should the developer take to improve the function's performance?

Increase the function's CPU

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda does not provide a direct setting to configure vCPU allocation. CPU power is determined indirectly through the memory setting, not through a standalone CPU control. Keyword tip: treat any answer that claims to configure CPU directly as a distractor, because Lambda has no such setting.
Your answer is incorrect
Increase the function's provisioned concurrency

Explanation

Incorrect. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments so that invocations do not experience cold-start delay. This setting reduces latency at the start of an invocation, but it does not change the amount of CPU power available once the function code is actually running. Keyword tip: provisioned concurrency and reserved concurrency solve cold-start and availability problems, not raw compute-speed problems.
Increase the function's timeout

Explanation

Incorrect. The timeout setting only controls the maximum duration a function is allowed to run before AWS Lambda terminates it. Increasing the timeout does not add computational power. A CPU-bound function will still run at the same speed, it will just be allowed to run longer before being cut off. Keyword tip: timeout controls the maximum execution duration, not the processing speed.
Correct answer
Increase the function's memory

Explanation

Correct. In AWS Lambda, the memory setting also determines the amount of virtual CPU, network bandwidth, and other resources allocated to the function. A developer can configure this memory setting anywhere from the smallest allowed value, 128 megabytes, up to the maximum of 10,240 megabytes. Increasing the memory value is the primary lever for improving performance in CPU-bound, network-bound, or memory-bound functions. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes a CPU-bound or resource-bound Lambda function that needs better performance, the correct action is almost always to increase memory.

AWS Lambda ties compute power directly to the memory setting: increasing memory proportionally increases the vCPU, network bandwidth, and other resources given to a function, so memory is the main lever for fixing CPU-bound, network-bound, or memory-bound performance issues. Timeout only changes how long a function is allowed to run before it is stopped; it does not make the function faster. Provisioned concurrency and reserved concurrency control cold-start latency and the number of available execution environments, not the compute power used during an already-running invocation. A developer must first identify whether the bottleneck is compute capacity, invocation availability, or execution duration, and then pick the matching control: memory for compute capacity, provisioned concurrency for cold starts, and timeout only as a safety limit.

Real-world example: at Bluecrest Foundation, a Lambda function that analyzes diagnostic imaging data to produce fast turnaround results for physicians was running slowly because it was limited to a low memory setting. A developer increased the function's memory allocation, which also increased its available vCPU, and the image-processing calculations completed significantly faster, allowing patient reports to be delivered within the required time window.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html

Question 39Incorrect

The database engineering team at Lumen Alliance, a water utility company that monitors smart water meters across a metropolitan service area, is designing a DynamoDB table to store real-time meter readings. The application must support reading 200 items per second using eventually consistent reads, and each item is 12 KB in size.

What value should be set for the table's provisioned throughput for reads?

Correct answer
300 Read Capacity Units

Explanation

Correct. For eventually consistent reads, one RCU supports two reads per second for an item up to 4 KB. A 12 KB item needs 3 RCUs per strongly consistent read, so eventually consistent reads need half that amount, which is 1.5 RCUs per read. Multiplying 1.5 RCUs by 200 reads per second gives 300 RCUs. Keyword tip: for eventually consistent reads, divide the rounded item size by 8 KB, which is double the 4 KB block, then multiply by the reads per second required.
600 Read Capacity Units

Explanation

Incorrect. This value equals 600 RCU, which matches the requirement for strongly consistent reads, not eventually consistent reads. A strongly consistent read of a 12 KB item needs 3 RCUs, because 12 KB divided by 4 KB equals 3. Multiplying 3 RCUs by 200 reads per second gives 600 RCUs. Keyword tip: strongly consistent reads always need double the RCUs of eventually consistent reads for the same item size and throughput.
Your answer is incorrect
1200 Read Capacity Units

Explanation

Incorrect. This value equals 1200 RCU, which matches the requirement for transactional reads, not eventually consistent reads. Transactional reads consume two RCUs per 4 KB block for each read per second. For a 12 KB item, that is 6 RCUs per read. Multiplying 6 RCUs by 200 reads per second gives 1200 RCUs. Keyword tip: transactional reads always require double the RCUs of strongly consistent reads for the same item size and throughput.
150 Read Capacity Units

Explanation

Incorrect. This value equals 150 RCU. This number results from using half the required read rate, 100 reads per second, instead of the correct 200 reads per second. Even though 1.5 RCU per read is correct for eventually consistent reads of a 12 KB item, multiplying by only 100 reads per second uses the wrong rate. Keyword tip: always use the exact reads-per-second value given in the scenario, not half of it.

Amazon DynamoDB provisioned capacity mode requires you to calculate read capacity units (RCUs) based on item size, read consistency type, and the number of reads per second. For strongly consistent reads, one RCU supports one read per second for an item up to 4 KB. For eventually consistent reads, one RCU supports two reads per second for an item up to 4 KB, so eventually consistent reads need half the RCUs of strongly consistent reads for the same item size. For transactional reads, DynamoDB doubles the RCU requirement of strongly consistent reads. To calculate the correct RCU value, round the item size up to the nearest 4 KB block, apply the RCU rule for the required consistency type, then multiply by the number of reads per second.

Practical example: Lumen Alliance, a water utility company, stores real-time readings from smart water meters in a DynamoDB table. The engineering team chooses eventually consistent reads for a monitoring dashboard because the dashboard does not need up-to-the-millisecond accuracy, and this choice cuts the required RCUs in half compared to strongly consistent reads. This reduces the provisioned throughput cost while still meeting the application's read requirements.

Question 40Incorrect

Configuring member access to user-specific folders inside a single Amazon S3 bucket, so that each user can reach only their own folder path, requires an IAM construct that works for every user without a separate policy per person. Brackenridge Robotics, a water utility company, needs this setup for its bucket named brackenridge-robotics-field-data: user-x must access only files in brackenridge-robotics-field-data/user/user-x/, user-y must access only files in brackenridge-robotics-field-data/user/user-y/, and this pattern must hold for every other team member.

As a Developer Associate, which IAM construct would you recommend so that a single, generic IAM policy statement can apply to all team members, without requiring a separate IAM policy for each individual user?

IAM policy condition

Explanation

Incorrect. The Condition element controls when a policy statement applies. For example, a condition can check "aws:username" against a fixed value like "johndoe". This still forces the administrator to write one condition value per user, so it does not create a single generic policy. Keyword tip: Condition blocks control the circumstances under which a policy applies. They do not dynamically insert the resource path itself.
IAM policy resource

Explanation

Incorrect. The Resource element lists the exact ARN or ARNs that a policy statement covers. On its own, the Resource element cannot change based on who is making the request. A hardcoded Resource element would still need one policy per user. Keyword tip: Resource defines what is being accessed, but it needs a policy variable to make that value change per user automatically.
Your answer is incorrect
IAM policy principal

Explanation

Incorrect. The Principal element identifies who is allowed or denied access to a resource. The Principal element is not valid inside an IAM identity-based policy. It only appears in resource-based policies and in the trust policies attached to IAM roles. The Principal element also has no mechanism for changing a resource path based on the requesting user. Keyword tip: Principal appears in trust policies and resource-based policies. Principal never appears in an identity-based policy attached directly to a user or group.
Correct answer
IAM policy variables

Explanation

Correct. IAM policy variables are placeholders inside a policy. AWS replaces these placeholders with values from the request context at the moment the policy is evaluated. The variable ${aws:username} is a common example. Using this variable, one policy attached to a group or role can grant each user access only to their own folder, such as brackenridge-robotics-field-data/user/${aws:username}/, without writing a separate policy for every user. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for one policy to serve many users with a per-user dynamic path, IAM policy variables such as ${aws:username} are the correct construct.

IAM policy variables let a single policy statement adjust its resource path based on information from the request context, most commonly the requesting user's identity through ${aws:username}. This removes the need to write one policy per user when the only difference between users is which folder they should reach. A Condition element is the right tool when access depends on a separate contextual attribute, such as source IP address or multi-factor authentication status, rather than on inserting the username into a path. A Resource element is correct when the ARN is fixed and already known in advance, and a Principal element belongs only in resource-based policies or role trust policies, never in an identity-based policy attached to a user or group. The core decision rule is this: if a scenario needs one reusable policy to scope many users to their own individual paths, IAM policy variables are the construct that makes that possible.

Real-world example: Brackenridge Robotics, a water utility company, stores field inspection photos and sensor logs from hundreds of technicians in one shared Amazon S3 bucket. Instead of an administrator manually writing and updating a separate IAM policy every time a technician joins or leaves the company, the security team attaches one IAM policy that uses ${aws:username} to build each technician's folder path automatically. New hires and departing employees are handled simply by adding or removing group membership, with no policy edits required.

Question 41Correct

The platform engineering team at Westfield Consolidated, a satellite communications provider headquartered in Denver, must deploy an update to an Amazon ECS service that powers the company's satellite telemetry dashboard using AWS CodeDeploy. The deployment must expose 10% of live production traffic to the new version first, and then, after a specified period of time, shift all remaining traffic to the new version.

Which ECS deployment strategy should the team use to meet these requirements?

Your answer is correct
Blue/green with canary

Explanation

Correct. The blue/green deployment type managed by AWS CodeDeploy supports a canary traffic-shifting strategy. In this strategy, traffic shifts in exactly two steps. First, a predefined percentage of traffic, such as 10%, is routed to the new task set. Then, after a specified wait interval measured in minutes, CodeDeploy shifts all remaining traffic to the new task set at once. This two-step pattern matches the requirement of exposing 10% of traffic first and then routing the rest after a period of time. Keyword tip: the pattern "shift X% first, then wait, then shift the rest" always identifies the canary strategy.
Blue/green with all at once

Explanation

Incorrect. The all-at-once strategy shifts 100% of traffic from the original task set to the updated task set immediately. There is no intermediate percentage step and no waiting period. Keyword tip: the phrase "all at once" signals an instant full cutover, which does not satisfy a phased traffic-shifting requirement.
Rolling update

Explanation

Incorrect. Rolling update is the native ECS deployment controller. It is not a CodeDeploy blue/green strategy. Rolling update replaces old tasks with new tasks gradually. It uses minimum healthy percent and maximum healthy percent settings to control the pace. Rolling update does not shift a specific percentage of live traffic, such as 10%, to a new task set in one defined step followed by a wait period. Keyword tip: the phrase "minimum/maximum healthy percent" with no traffic-shifting percentage points to the native ECS rolling update type, not CodeDeploy blue/green.
Blue/green with linear

Explanation

Incorrect. The linear strategy shifts traffic in multiple equal increments. Each increment is separated by an equal number of minutes. For example, traffic might shift by 10% every 3 minutes until it reaches 100%. This differs from the canary pattern, which uses a single initial percentage followed by one final shift of the remainder. Keyword tip: the phrase "equal increments at equal time intervals" identifies the linear strategy, not the two-step canary pattern.

AWS CodeDeploy blue/green deployments for Amazon ECS support three traffic-shifting strategies. The canary strategy shifts traffic in two steps: an initial percentage, then a wait period, then the rest. The linear strategy shifts traffic in several equal steps spaced at equal time intervals. The all-at-once strategy performs a single, immediate full cutover with no gradual exposure. The native ECS rolling update controller is a separate mechanism entirely; it replaces tasks gradually based on healthy percent settings, but it has no concept of percentage-based traffic shifting. When a scenario describes an initial small percentage of traffic exposure followed by a delay and then a full shift to the remainder, canary is the correct choice.

Consider this scenario: Westfield Consolidated operates a satellite telemetry dashboard that ground station operators rely on around the clock. Before the platform engineering team fully switches operators over to a new backend version, they want to confirm the update behaves correctly under real production load with minimal risk. By using a canary strategy, the team exposes only 10% of traffic to the new version, monitors for errors during the wait period, and then completes the cutover once confidence is established.

Question 42Correct

A routine internal security audit revealed that traffic between the application tier and the database tier was traveling across the public internet, prompting immediate concern from the compliance team. The audit was performed at Northbridge Continental, a video conferencing SaaS company with over 5 million monthly active users, whose CRM application runs on Amazon EC2 instances backed by an Amazon DynamoDB database tier.

As a developer associate on the team, which of the following would you suggest as an optimal solution for providing communication between the EC2 instances and DynamoDB without using the public internet?

Create a NAT gateway to provide the necessary communication channel between the EC2 instances and DynamoDB

Explanation

Incorrect. A NAT gateway allows instances in a private subnet to start outbound connections to the internet or to other services. A NAT gateway does not remove the need for internet-based routing when accessing DynamoDB. Amazon EC2 and Amazon DynamoDB are both AWS services, so using a NAT gateway adds cost and complexity without meeting the requirement to avoid the public internet. Keyword tip: NAT gateway supports outbound internet access from private subnets, not private service-to-service connectivity.
Create an internet gateway to provide the necessary communication channel between the EC2 instances and DynamoDB

Explanation

Incorrect. An internet gateway allows resources inside a VPC to communicate with the public internet. An internet gateway is required when instances need a public IP address to be reached from outside the VPC. Using an internet gateway here would send EC2-to-DynamoDB traffic across the public internet, which is exactly what the scenario needs to avoid. Keyword tip: internet gateway provides public internet connectivity, the opposite of what this scenario requires.
Your answer is correct
Configure a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB that will provide the required internal access without using the public internet

Explanation

Correct. A VPC gateway endpoint for DynamoDB routes all traffic between the EC2 instances and DynamoDB through the Amazon internal network. Traffic does not travel across the public internet. The application code does not need any changes because the DynamoDB endpoint name stays the same. Endpoint policies can add further access restrictions for extra security. Keyword tip: when a question asks for private connectivity between EC2 or Lambda and DynamoDB or S3 without using the public internet, the answer is a VPC endpoint — a gateway endpoint for S3 and DynamoDB, or an interface endpoint for most other services.
Use a virtual private network (VPN) to route all DynamoDB network traffic through the organization's own corporate network infrastructure

Explanation

Incorrect. Routing DynamoDB traffic through a corporate VPN keeps the traffic off the public internet. This approach adds extra latency, limits available bandwidth, and depends on the availability of the corporate network. A native AWS solution avoids these trade-offs and scales better. Keyword tip: VPN routing through on-premises infrastructure is a workaround, not the AWS-native best practice for private service access.

This question tests knowledge of private connectivity options between compute resources in a VPC and AWS-managed services such as DynamoDB. A VPC gateway endpoint is the AWS-native solution for keeping DynamoDB and Amazon S3 traffic entirely inside the Amazon network, without needing an internet gateway, a NAT gateway, or a VPN tunnel. Endpoint policies let a team add additional access controls to the endpoint. A NAT gateway and an internet gateway both exist to enable or control internet-bound traffic, which works against the goal of keeping traffic off the public internet. VPN routing through corporate infrastructure can technically avoid the public internet, but it adds latency, bandwidth limits, and dependency on external network availability, making it a weaker choice than a VPC endpoint. When a scenario calls for private, low-latency, and cost-efficient access to an AWS service from inside a VPC, check first whether that service supports a VPC endpoint before considering a NAT gateway, an internet gateway, or a VPN workaround.

A similar situation: Northbridge Continental, a video conferencing SaaS company, stores call metadata and customer account records in DynamoDB while running its CRM logic on EC2 instances. After an audit flagged the public internet path as a compliance risk, the platform team configures a VPC gateway endpoint for DynamoDB so that all database traffic stays inside the AWS network, satisfying both security requirements and customer trust expectations without re-architecting the application.

Question 43Correct

The DevOps engineering team supporting Wrenfield Associates, an industrial manufacturing company, is building a microservices application that runs on Amazon ECS to manage production-line telemetry data. The team's release process requires a manual sign-off from a senior engineer before any new code reaches the production environment.

What is the BEST way to enforce this manual approval step using AWS CodePipeline?

Disable the stage transition to allow manual approval

Explanation

Incorrect. Disabling the stage transition requires a person to manually re-enable the transition later in the AWS Management Console. This manual step can be forgotten. If the transition is re-enabled without an actual review taking place, the deployment proceeds without any real approval. Keyword tip: treat manual stage transition toggles as an unreliable workaround, not as a built-in approval mechanism.
Your answer is correct
Use an approval action in a stage before deployment

Explanation

Correct. AWS CodePipeline supports adding a manual approval action inside a stage that runs before the deployment stage. This approval action stops the pipeline at that point. The pipeline stays stopped until an IAM principal with the required permissions approves the action or rejects it. If no one responds within seven days, or if the action is rejected, the pipeline execution stops and is treated as failed. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires a person to sign off before a production deployment, look for a manual approval action placed in a stage before the deployment stage.
Use an Amazon SNS notification from the deployment stage

Explanation

Incorrect. An Amazon SNS notification sent from the deployment stage only alerts someone after the deployment has already started or already finished. This notification does not stop the pipeline and does not block the deployment from happening. Keyword tip: SNS notifications inform people about pipeline events, but they do not gate or pause pipeline execution.
Disable a stage just prior to the deployment stage

Explanation

Incorrect. Disabling a stage that runs just before the deployment stage stops that stage from running at all. This is not the same as pausing for review. That earlier stage might perform a needed function, such as a build step or a test step, and skipping it removes that function entirely. Keyword tip: disabling a stage means skipping its execution completely, not pausing the pipeline for a human decision.

This question tests knowledge of how to add a human review checkpoint inside an automated CI/CD pipeline using AWS CodePipeline. The correct mechanism is a manual approval action placed inside a stage that runs before the deployment stage that targets production. When the pipeline reaches that action, it stops running until an authorized IAM principal approves the action or rejects it, and the pipeline execution fails automatically if no one responds within seven days. Other approaches in this scenario, such as disabling stages, toggling stage transitions, or sending SNS notifications, either fail to actually stop the pipeline or depend on a manual step that a person can forget or skip. When a pipeline design requires sign-off before a sensitive deployment, place a dedicated approval action in a stage immediately before that deployment stage.

Use case: Wrenfield Associates operates production-line systems where a faulty deployment could disrupt manufacturing output. The DevOps team places a manual approval action in the pipeline stage right before the production deployment stage, so a senior engineer must review and approve every release before it reaches the factory-facing services. This gives the team an audited, reliable checkpoint instead of relying on someone remembering to re-enable a disabled stage transition.

Question 44Correct

Foxglove Group needs to build an AWS Lambda function that consumes real-time parcel-scan events from an Amazon Kinesis data stream and updates package status without producing duplicate delivery records, since Foxglove Group operates as a national courier and parcel service tracking millions of packages across its distribution network. A developer configures the function to parse each scan event, but whenever an event is missing an expected field, the function throws an unhandled exception and exits.

Operations staff later notice that the same scan records appear more than once in the downstream tracking system that consumes the Lambda function's output. When the developer inspects the raw Kinesis stream directly, without the Lambda function attached, no duplicate records exist in the stream itself.

What is the reason for the duplicate records?

The Lambda function is not keeping up with the amount of data coming from the stream

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda automatically scales how it reads from a Kinesis data stream. Lambda processes multiple shards in parallel and adds more concurrent executions when the stream carries more data. If Lambda falls behind the incoming data rate, this shows up as increasing iterator age, not duplicate records. Falling behind on throughput does not make Lambda reprocess the same batch of records. Keyword tip: Throughput or scaling problems appear as increasing iterator age, not duplicate delivery.
The Lambda event source used asynchronous invocation, resulting in duplicate records

Explanation

Incorrect. The Kinesis event source mapping polls the stream on Lambda's behalf. The event source mapping invokes the Lambda function synchronously for each batch of records. The event source mapping does not use asynchronous invocation for Kinesis. Asynchronous invocation is not the cause of the duplicate records in this scenario. Keyword tip: Stream-based event sources, such as Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams, always use synchronous, poll-based invocation through the event source mapping.
The Lambda function did not advance the Kinesis stream pointer to the next record after the error

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda does not expose a stream pointer that a developer can control from application code. The event source mapping tracks the shard iterator position internally. The event source mapping advances the shard iterator position only after a batch is processed successfully. Keyword tip: Shard position tracking is managed internally by the event source mapping, not by the function's code.
Your answer is correct
The Lambda function did not handle the error, and the Lambda service attempted to reprocess the data

Explanation

Correct. When a Lambda function returns an error while processing a batch of records from a Kinesis data stream, the Lambda service does not skip the failing batch automatically. Instead, the Lambda service retries the same batch until the batch succeeds, until the batch expires based on the configured maximum record age, or until the batch is skipped because of a configured retry limit or bisect-on-error setting. In this scenario, the function does not handle the missing-field error inside its own code, so the Lambda service retries the same batch, and this retry behavior produces records that appear duplicated in the downstream tracking system. Keyword tip: An unhandled function error on a stream-based event source causes batch-level retries, which is the classic cause of duplicate processing.

This question tests understanding of how the Lambda event source mapping handles function errors when reading from an Amazon Kinesis data stream. The event source mapping invokes Lambda synchronously for each batch of records, and it only advances its position in the stream after a batch finishes successfully. If the function raises an unhandled error partway through a batch, the event source mapping retries the entire batch instead of skipping it, based on the configured maximum record age and retry settings. This retry behavior, not a throughput problem and not an invocation-type misconfiguration, is the classic cause of records that appear duplicated only after passing through the Lambda function.

A similar situation: Foxglove Group's tracking pipeline processes scan events for parcels moving through regional sorting hubs, and a single malformed scan event without proper error handling could cause an entire batch of legitimate scans to be reprocessed and double-counted in the delivery status system. To prevent this, the development team should catch parsing errors inside the function, route unprocessable records to a dead-letter destination, and configure bisect-on-error so a single bad record does not force the whole batch to retry repeatedly.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/invocation-retries.html

Question 45Correct

Multiple consumer applications are experiencing a delivery lag when they read automobile health-status data concurrently from the same Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream. Stonebridge Continental, an online marketplace that also operates a taxi ride-hailing service connecting drivers and riders, collects this vehicle health data from its fleet and needs to reduce the delay between the data producers and the data consumers.

As a Developer Associate, which of the following options would you suggest to improve performance for this use case?

Swap out Kinesis Data Streams with SQS Standard queues

Explanation

Incorrect. SQS Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. SQS Standard queues do not natively support multiple independent consumer applications each reading the full stream of records, because a message is typically removed from visibility once a consumer reads it. This behavior makes SQS Standard unsuitable for fanning out the same data to several concurrent analytics consumers. Keyword tip: SQS uses a point-to-point, competing-consumers model, not a multi-consumer stream-replay model like Kinesis Data Streams.
Swap out Kinesis Data Streams with Kinesis Data Firehose

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed delivery service. Kinesis Data Firehose loads streaming data into destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, or Splunk. Kinesis Data Firehose does not allow multiple independent applications to consume and read the same stream concurrently the way Kinesis Data Streams does. Keyword tip: Firehose is for delivery into a data store, not for custom multi-consumer stream processing.
Swap out Kinesis Data Streams with SQS FIFO queues

Explanation

Incorrect. SQS FIFO queues guarantee exactly-once processing and strict message order for a single logical consumer group. SQS FIFO queues do not let multiple independent consumer applications read the same stream of records in parallel at high throughput. Moving away from Kinesis Data Streams would also force Stonebridge Continental to redesign its entire multi-consumer architecture. Keyword tip: SQS FIFO solves ordering and duplicate prevention, not multi-consumer fanout throughput.
Your answer is correct
Use the Enhanced Fan-Out feature of Kinesis Data Streams

Explanation

Correct. By default, each shard's 2 MB/second output is shared among all consuming applications. This shared throughput causes contention and delivery lag when multiple consumers read from the same stream. The Enhanced Fan-Out feature gives each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/second read throughput per shard, and this dedicated throughput scales automatically with the number of shards, removing the shared-throughput bottleneck. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes multiple parallel consumers on Kinesis Data Streams with throughput or lag problems, Enhanced Fan-Out is the answer.

This question tests understanding of how to scale read throughput in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams when multiple consumer applications need to process the same stream at the same time. By default, a shard's 2 MB/second read throughput is shared among all consumers. As more consumer applications are added, each consumer receives a smaller effective share of that throughput, which causes delivery lag. The Enhanced Fan-Out feature solves this problem by giving each registered consumer its own dedicated 2 MB/second-per-shard pipe, using an HTTP/2 push mechanism instead of the shared pull model. Switching to SQS Standard, SQS FIFO, or Kinesis Data Firehose does not solve this problem, because none of those services support the same multi-consumer, replayable stream-processing model that Kinesis Data Streams provides.

Use case: Stonebridge Continental's ride-hailing service streams vehicle health telemetry from its taxi fleet into a single Kinesis Data Streams stream. Multiple internal teams, such as predictive maintenance, safety monitoring, and driver-performance analytics, each run a separate consumer application against this same stream. As Stonebridge Continental adds more consumer applications, engineers register each one as an Enhanced Fan-Out consumer so every team gets its own dedicated 2 MB/second-per-shard throughput, keeping all consumers current without competing for shared bandwidth.

Question 46Correct

Union Systems currently stores transaction records and customer profile data in Amazon S3 buckets, relying on Amazon S3's default encryption settings to protect data at rest. The payment processing company's compliance team now requires an AWS managed encryption solution that still gives Union Systems full control to create, rotate, and remove the encryption keys used to protect this data.

As a Developer Associate, which of the following would you recommend to address this use case?

Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3)

Explanation

Incorrect. With Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3-Managed Keys (SSE-S3), AWS manages and automatically rotates the master key used to encrypt each object's data key. Union Systems has no visibility into these keys. Union Systems cannot create, rotate, or delete these keys. Keyword tip: SSE-S3 is the simplest, fully AWS-managed option with zero customer control over key management; use it only when key control is not a requirement.
Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys (SSE-C)

Explanation

Incorrect. With Server-Side Encryption with Customer-Provided Keys (SSE-C), Union Systems supplies the encryption key with each request. Amazon S3 performs the encryption and decryption using that key. Amazon S3 does not store, manage, rotate, or delete the key on Union Systems' behalf. Union Systems would need to build and manage the entire key lifecycle process outside of AWS, which does not meet the requirement for an AWS managed solution. Keyword tip: SSE-C means "you bring the key and manage it yourself," which contradicts a requirement for an AWS managed key lifecycle.
Server-Side Encryption with Secrets Manager

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Secrets Manager stores, rotates, and retrieves secrets such as database credentials and API keys. AWS Secrets Manager does not encrypt S3 objects. AWS Secrets Manager cannot create, rotate, or disable S3 encryption keys. Keyword tip: Secrets Manager relates to secret and credential rotation, not object-level server-side encryption for S3.
Your answer is correct
Server-Side Encryption with Customer Master Keys (CMKs) Stored in AWS Key Management Service (SSE-KMS)

Explanation

Correct. Server-Side Encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS) lets Union Systems use a customer-managed customer master key (CMK) instead of the AWS default key. Union Systems owns this CMK. Union Systems can create the CMK, rotate the CMK, disable the CMK, and delete the CMK. Union Systems can also set granular key policies and IAM permissions, and can audit key usage through AWS CloudTrail. AWS KMS still manages the underlying cryptographic infrastructure, so Union Systems gets an AWS managed service with full key lifecycle control. Keyword tip: when a scenario mentions "full control over key lifecycle" plus "AWS managed service," think SSE-KMS with a customer-managed CMK.

This question tests knowledge of the Amazon S3 server-side encryption options and which option gives the customer control over the encryption key lifecycle. SSE-S3 puts key management fully with AWS, so the customer has no control. SSE-C puts key management fully with the customer, so AWS provides no managed key service. SSE-KMS with a customer-managed CMK balances both needs: AWS KMS manages the cryptographic operations and infrastructure, while the customer retains full control to create, rotate, disable, and delete the CMK, and to audit its usage through AWS CloudTrail. AWS Secrets Manager is unrelated to S3 object encryption, since it only manages application secrets like database credentials and API keys. When a scenario requires both AWS-managed infrastructure and customer control over key creation, rotation, and deletion, SSE-KMS with a customer-managed CMK is the correct choice.

Real-world example: A payment processing company like Union Systems must meet strict compliance requirements such as PCI DSS, which often require the ability to prove control over encryption key rotation and revocation for stored cardholder and transaction data. By using SSE-KMS with a customer-managed CMK, Union Systems can disable or delete a specific key immediately if a security incident occurs, without waiting on AWS to manage that action, while still avoiding the operational burden of building its own key management system.

Question 47Incorrect

The release engineering team at Truenorth Enterprises, a theme park operator whose ride-reservation platform runs on AWS Lambda, needs a seamless way to roll back to an older version of a Lambda function whenever a new deployment causes problems.

Which of the following solutions offers the LEAST operational overhead?

Use an Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policy that can point to the different Lambda function versions

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon Route 53 weighted routing policies distribute DNS traffic across multiple resources, such as EC2 instances or load balancers. Route 53 does not have a mechanism to send invocations to a specific Lambda function version. Route 53 works at the DNS level, not at the Lambda invocation level. Keyword tip: if a question mentions DNS-level traffic distribution across domain names, think Route 53. If it asks about routing to a specific Lambda version, Route 53 is not the answer.
Your answer is incorrect
Use Lambda function layers that can point to the different versions

Explanation

Incorrect. Lambda layers package and share libraries, custom runtimes, or other dependencies across multiple functions. Layers reduce deployment package size and reduce code duplication. Layers are not designed to point to or switch between different versions of a function's own code, so layers cannot implement rollback. Keyword tip: layers are for shared dependencies, not for version pointing or rollback.
Correct answer
Use a Lambda function alias that can point to the different versions

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda alias is a pointer with its own stable Amazon Resource Name (ARN). The alias can be repointed to any published function version at any time. Repointing the alias causes an instant, seamless rollback because client code keeps invoking the same ARN. This approach needs no extra infrastructure, no deployment pipeline, and no routing configuration, which makes it the lowest-overhead solution. Keyword tip: when a question describes a stable ARN that clients invoke while the version behind it changes, think Lambda alias.
Use AWS CodeDeploy to configure blue/green deployments for the different Lambda function versions

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS CodeDeploy performs a blue/green-style traffic shift, using canary, linear, or all-at-once configurations, to move traffic toward a new Lambda function version during a deployment. Once a deployment finishes, CodeDeploy does not offer a built-in way to shift traffic back to the previous version without starting a new deployment. CodeDeploy also requires extra setup, including deployment groups, hooks, and a CodeDeploy application, compared to simply repointing an alias. Keyword tip: CodeDeploy manages traffic shifting during a deployment, not a simple after-the-fact rollback pointer change.

This question tests knowledge of Lambda versioning and aliasing as the mechanism for low-overhead rollback. A Lambda version is an immutable, numbered snapshot of the function code and configuration. A Lambda alias is a mutable pointer that targets one specific version, and a developer can move the alias to an older version instantly without changing the ARN that client code invokes. Route 53 weighted routing policies work at the DNS level and cannot target Lambda versions directly, and Lambda layers store shared dependencies rather than different versions of the function's own code. AWS CodeDeploy shifts traffic toward a new version during a deployment but does not provide a lightweight built-in rollback pointer after the deployment completes, which makes alias repointing the simplest and lowest-overhead solution.

Practical example: At Truenorth Enterprises, the Lambda function that processes ride-reservation bookings serves guests across every park location. If a new deployment introduces booking errors, the release engineering team can immediately move the production alias back to the last stable version. This restores service within seconds, without redeploying code and without configuring a new CodeDeploy pipeline.

Question 48Incorrect

Ridgewood Analytics currently uses Amazon SQS to decouple the backend of its guest-facing application, which generates personalized park-visit memes for theme park visitors. The consumers of the RidgewoodMemeQueue currently use short polling and query the queue continuously to keep throughput high.

This approach is proving to be costly and resource intensive because of a large number of empty responses. A developer at Ridgewood Analytics has been asked to review the system and propose changes that can reduce costs and the number of empty responses.

What would be the BEST approach to minimizing cost?

Set the RidgewoodMemeQueue's MessageRetentionPeriod attribute to 20 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. MessageRetentionPeriod controls how long Amazon SQS keeps a message in the queue if the message is not deleted. The default value is 4 days. The maximum value is 14 days. This attribute does not affect polling frequency. This attribute does not affect empty responses. Keyword tip: MessageRetentionPeriod controls message lifespan, not polling cost.
Set the RidgewoodMemeQueue's VisibilityTimeout attribute to 20 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. VisibilityTimeout controls how long a message stays hidden from other consumers after a consumer receives the message. This attribute prevents duplicate processing of the same message. This attribute does not control how often consumers poll the queue. This attribute does not reduce empty responses. Keyword tip: VisibilityTimeout prevents duplicate message processing; it does not reduce polling cost.
Correct answer
Set the RidgewoodMemeQueue's ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds attribute to 20 seconds

Explanation

Correct. Setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds to a value greater than 0 seconds, up to a maximum of 20 seconds, turns on long polling. With long polling, the ReceiveMessage call waits for a message to arrive instead of returning an empty response right away. This behavior reduces the number of empty responses. This behavior also reduces the number of API calls, which lowers cost. Keyword tip: ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds is the queue attribute that turns on long polling.
Your answer is incorrect
Set the DelaySeconds parameter of a message to 20 seconds

Explanation

Incorrect. The DelaySeconds parameter delays how long a new message stays invisible to consumers after it is sent. This parameter does not change how consumers poll the queue. This parameter does not reduce empty responses. Keyword tip: DelaySeconds controls message delivery delay, not polling behavior.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon SQS polling mechanisms and how to use them to reduce cost. By default, SQS uses short polling. Short polling queries only a subset of the queue's servers, and this behavior can return an empty response even when messages exist elsewhere in the queue. Each empty response is still a billed request, so frequent short polling wastes money. Long polling fixes this problem: when ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds is set to a value between 1 and 20 seconds, the ReceiveMessage call waits until a message arrives or the timeout expires, instead of returning immediately. This reduces the number of empty responses and reduces the number of billed requests. As a general rule, choose long polling for cost optimization unless the application needs a near-instant empty response when the queue has no messages.

Consider this scenario: Ridgewood Analytics runs a meme-generation feature that theme park visitors use heavily during peak park hours but rarely use overnight. With short polling, the consumer application keeps calling ReceiveMessage at a fixed rate around the clock, and most of those calls return empty during low-traffic hours. By switching the RidgewoodMemeQueue to long polling with ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds set to 20 seconds, Ridgewood Analytics cuts the number of wasted empty-response calls significantly, which lowers the SQS bill without changing how quickly guests receive their memes during busy periods.

Question 49Correct

Lumen Regional, an agricultural technology company, manages its field-sensor infrastructure using AWS CloudFormation. The team has built a template that provisions a stack containing a VPC and a subnet used by soil-monitoring devices across the company's farm network.

The subnet's output value must now be made available to a separate CloudFormation stack that deploys the data-ingestion pipeline.

As a Developer Associate at Lumen Regional, which of the following options would you suggest to provide this information to the other stack?

Use Fn::Transform

Explanation

Incorrect. The Fn::Transform intrinsic function specifies a macro. This macro performs custom processing on part of a template. Fn::Transform does not share output values between stacks. Keyword tip: Associate Fn::Transform with macros and custom template processing, not with cross-stack references.
Use the 'Expose' field in the Outputs section of the stack's template

Explanation

Incorrect. 'Expose' is not a valid CloudFormation Outputs attribute. This option is a fabricated distractor. Keyword tip: The only valid attribute used to make an output shareable across stacks is Export, not Expose.
Your answer is correct
Use the 'Export' field in the Outputs section of the stack's template

Explanation

Correct. To share information between stacks, the producing stack must declare the value in its Outputs section. The producing stack uses the Export field for this declaration. The Export field makes the output value available by name to any other stack in the same AWS account and AWS Region. Keyword tip: The word 'Export' in the Outputs section is the signal for making a value shareable across stacks.
Use Fn::ImportValue

Explanation

Incorrect. Fn::ImportValue is used in the consuming stack's template. Fn::ImportValue imports a value that another stack has already exported. Fn::ImportValue does not publish or expose the value itself. The subnet's stack must export the output first, before another stack can use Fn::ImportValue to read it. Keyword tip: Fn::ImportValue is the 'read' side of cross-stack references, and Export is the 'write' side.

This question tests knowledge of CloudFormation cross-stack references. A cross-stack reference lets one stack publish a resource attribute, such as a subnet ID, so that other stacks in the same AWS account and Region can consume it. The producing stack declares the value using the Export field in its Outputs section. The consuming stack then retrieves that value using the Fn::ImportValue intrinsic function. Fn::Transform is unrelated because it is used for macros and template-wide custom processing, and 'Expose' is not a real CloudFormation attribute.

Consider this scenario: Lumen Regional's network team provisions a VPC and subnet stack that supports its soil-monitoring sensor network. A separate team builds a data-ingestion pipeline stack that needs the subnet ID to place its processing resources correctly. The network team exports the subnet ID as a named output, and the data-ingestion stack imports that value with Fn::ImportValue, keeping the two stacks decoupled while still sharing the required infrastructure detail.

Question 50Correct

A sudden spike in onboard security-camera footage and passenger-flow sensor readings has overwhelmed the existing hourly batch reporting job, delaying incident alerts by several hours. Ashgrove Logistics, a cruise line operator with a fleet operations center in Miami, must ingest several terabytes of data every hour from thousands of distributed shipboard and port sources.

Messages arrive continuously, 24 hours a day, and must be delivered in real time to support security analysis and live operational dashboards.

Which approach will meet these requirements?

Your answer is correct
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with the Kinesis Client Library to ingest and deliver messages

Explanation

Correct. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is built to collect and process large volumes of streaming data in real time from many distributed producers. An application built with the Kinesis Client Library (KCL) reads records as they arrive. This application can then feed live dashboards, alerting systems, or downstream analytics with very low latency. Keyword tip: continuous, high-throughput, real-time ingestion from many sources for live analytics or dashboards points to Kinesis Data Streams.
Use the Amazon S3 API to write messages to an S3 bucket, then process the messages by using Amazon Redshift

Explanation

Incorrect. Writing messages to Amazon S3 creates batch-oriented, file-based storage. This storage does not support real-time streaming. Amazon Redshift is a data warehouse built for running analytical queries over data that is already loaded, not for consuming live message streams from S3. This combination adds latency that does not meet the real-time requirement for security analysis and live dashboards. Keyword tip: S3 combined with Redshift signals batch analytics, not real-time stream processing.
Use AWS Data Pipeline to automate the movement and transformation of data

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Data Pipeline orchestrates and automates the movement and transformation of data between AWS services on a scheduled or batch basis. AWS Data Pipeline does not provide real-time stream ingestion and delivery to dashboards. This scenario requires continuous, low-latency ingestion and processing, not scheduled data transformation. Keyword tip: Data Pipeline points to scheduled ETL or batch data movement workflows, not real-time streaming.
Send the messages to an Amazon SQS queue, then process the messages by using a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon SQS is designed to decouple application components through queuing. Amazon SQS is not designed to ingest and continuously process high-volume streaming data for real-time analytics. Using a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances to poll and process messages from the queue would be costly and hard to scale elastically as data volume grows. This approach would also add latency and could run into SQS message size limits. Keyword tip: SQS points to decoupling and point-to-point processing, not real-time streaming analytics.

This question tests whether a candidate can identify the correct AWS service for continuous, high-throughput, real-time data ingestion versus services built for batch processing or simple decoupling. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, paired with the Kinesis Client Library, is the standard choice when many distributed producers send large volumes of data continuously and consumers need to process that data with very low latency. Amazon SQS is best for decoupling components and delivering messages point-to-point, not for continuous stream analytics. Amazon S3 combined with Amazon Redshift supports batch analytics on data already at rest, and AWS Data Pipeline supports scheduled ETL workflows, so neither fits a real-time requirement. The decision logic is to match the stated latency and throughput requirements, continuous and real-time and high-volume, to the service built specifically for streaming data.

Consider this scenario: Ashgrove Logistics operates security cameras, access-control sensors, and passenger-flow monitors across a fleet of cruise ships and port terminals. Each device streams events continuously, and the fleet operations center needs to see potential security incidents on live dashboards within seconds, not hours. By ingesting this data with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and consuming it with an application built on the Kinesis Client Library, the operations team gets near real-time visibility instead of waiting for a batch job to finish.

Question 51Incorrect

Oakhaven Labs, a pharmaceutical research organization based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, runs a hybrid drug-discovery application that combines Amazon EC2 instances with on-premises servers located in its wet-lab facility. The on-premises servers host mission-critical compound-screening software, and a developer at Oakhaven Labs needs to collect both performance metrics and application logs from those servers using Amazon CloudWatch.

Which approach lets the developer accomplish this?

Install the CloudWatch agent on the on-premises servers and specify an IAM role with permissions to CloudWatch

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM role cannot be attached to an on-premises server, because IAM roles depend on the AWS instance metadata service. The instance metadata service only exists on AWS resources, such as EC2 instances or Lambda functions. An on-premises server must use IAM user credentials instead, meaning an access key and a secret access key. Keyword tip: when a question combines the words "on-premises" and "IAM role" in the same option, treat that option as incorrect, because roles only work on AWS compute resources.
Correct answer
Install the CloudWatch agent on the on-premises servers and specify IAM credentials with permissions to CloudWatch

Explanation

Correct. The CloudWatch agent can be installed on an on-premises server. During setup, the developer configures the agent with IAM user credentials that grant CloudWatch permissions. These credentials let the on-premises server send both metrics and log files to CloudWatch, so the on-premises server appears in the same dashboards as the EC2 instances. Keyword tip: the phrase "CloudWatch agent" combined with "on-premises" and "IAM credentials" (not "IAM role") is the standard correct pattern for hybrid monitoring.
Your answer is incorrect
Install an AWS SDK on the on-premises servers that automatically sends logs to CloudWatch

Explanation

Incorrect. An AWS SDK can send custom log data to CloudWatch Logs, but this approach requires the developer to write and maintain custom code. This approach also does not automatically collect system-level performance metrics the way the CloudWatch agent does. The CloudWatch agent is the purpose-built, managed solution for this task, so building a custom SDK integration is unnecessary extra work. Keyword tip: if an option describes writing custom SDK code to do what a managed agent already does, treat that option as a less efficient distractor.
Write a batch script that uses system utilities to collect performance metrics and application logs, then upload the metrics and logs to CloudWatch

Explanation

Incorrect. Writing a batch script that uses system utilities to collect metrics and logs, then uploading that data to CloudWatch, duplicates functionality that the CloudWatch agent already provides. The CloudWatch agent includes built-in retry logic, data buffering, and standardized metric formatting, so a custom script adds maintenance burden without any benefit. Keyword tip: any option describing a custom script or manual upload process for a task that has a native AWS agent is almost always the wrong choice.

This question tests how to extend Amazon CloudWatch monitoring into a hybrid environment that includes on-premises servers. The CloudWatch agent is the correct tool because it collects both system metrics and log files from any server, whether that server runs on EC2 or on-premises. An EC2 instance can use an IAM role through an instance profile, because AWS automatically issues and rotates temporary credentials for that instance. An on-premises server cannot use an IAM role, because IAM roles depend on the AWS instance metadata service, which does not exist outside AWS; the on-premises server must instead use long-term IAM user credentials, meaning an access key and a secret access key, configured directly in the CloudWatch agent.

Use case: At Oakhaven Labs, the compound-screening servers in the wet-lab facility run continuously and must stay under close monitoring, because a failure could halt an active drug-discovery experiment. A developer installs the CloudWatch agent on each on-premises server and configures it with IAM user credentials scoped to only the CloudWatch permissions it needs. This setup lets the operations team view metrics and logs from the on-premises lab servers in the same CloudWatch dashboards used for the EC2-based analysis pipeline, giving a single unified view of the hybrid application.

Question 52Correct

Extending a web application's deployment to a second AWS Region without adding unnecessary operational work is the current goal for Overlook Regional, a regional banking institution headquartered in Denver, Colorado. The bank runs its web application on Amazon EC2 instances built from a custom Amazon Machine Image (AMI) and uses AWS CloudFormation to deploy the application, which is currently running in the us-east-1 Region.

The team now wants to extend the deployment to the us-west-1 Region. During an initial attempt to create an AWS CloudFormation stack in us-west-1, the stack creation fails, and an error message indicates that the AMI ID does not exist. A developer at Overlook Regional is tasked with resolving this error using an approach that minimizes operational complexity.

Which action should the developer take?

Create a new AMI in the us-west-1 Region and update the CloudFormation template with the new AMI ID.

Explanation

Incorrect. Building a brand-new AMI from scratch in us-west-1 takes more time than copying an existing AMI. This method also risks configuration drift, meaning the new AMI could differ from the original AMI. Because of this extra time and risk, this method does not meet the requirement to minimize operational effort. Keyword tip: recreating an image instead of copying it is a signal of unnecessary extra complexity.
Your answer is correct
Copy the AMI from the us-east-1 Region to the us-west-1 Region and use the new AMI ID in the CloudFormation template.

Explanation

Correct. An AMI is a Region-specific resource. An AMI ID that is valid in us-east-1 does not exist in us-west-1. The AWS-recommended way to make an existing AMI available in another Region is to copy the AMI to that Region. After the copy completes, the developer references the new AMI ID in the CloudFormation template used for that Region. Keyword tip: when an AMI ID error appears in a new Region, think "copy the AMI" as the lowest-effort fix.
Use AWS Lambda to create an AMI in the us-west-1 Region during stack creation.

Explanation

Incorrect. Using AWS Lambda to create an AMI during stack creation adds extra complexity. This approach needs a custom CloudFormation resource and a Lambda function to run the AMI creation logic. The AMI created this way is not guaranteed to match the original AMI exactly. Keyword tip: any option that requires building new automation logic to solve a simple cross-Region resource problem is usually more complex than necessary.
Modify the CloudFormation template to refer to the AMI in the us-east-1 Region.

Explanation

Incorrect. An AMI is a Region-specific resource. A CloudFormation stack in us-west-1 cannot reference an AMI ID that only exists in us-east-1, so this template edit does not fix the error. Keyword tip: remember that an AMI, unlike some AWS resources, does not have a cross-Region identifier and must be explicitly copied to be used in another Region.

An AMI is a Region-specific resource in AWS. To deploy the same EC2-based application in a new Region using AWS CloudFormation, the AMI must first exist in that target Region. The lowest-effort, AWS-recommended approach is to copy the existing AMI to the target Region and reference the new AMI ID in the template. Rebuilding the AMI from scratch, referencing it across Regions directly, or adding custom Lambda-based automation to generate a new AMI are all more complex alternatives that either fail technically or introduce unnecessary operational overhead.

Practical example: Overlook Regional needs to run its loan-processing web application in both us-east-1 and us-west-1 to meet its disaster recovery requirements as a regional banking institution. Instead of manually rebuilding the custom AMI in us-west-1, the developer copies the existing AMI from us-east-1 to us-west-1 and updates the CloudFormation template with the new AMI ID, allowing the stack to deploy successfully with minimal extra work.

Question 53Incorrect

The application development team at Everstone Technologies, a nonprofit disaster-relief organization that coordinates emergency logistics across multiple regions, is building a microservices application that will use Docker containers on Amazon ECS. The architecture includes 6 distinct services, and each service requires specific permissions to access various AWS services.

What is the MOST secure way to grant the services the necessary permissions?

Correct answer
Create six separate IAM roles, each containing the required permissions for the associated ECS service, then configure each ECS task definition to reference the associated IAM role

Explanation

Correct. IAM Roles for Amazon ECS Tasks let a distinct IAM role be attached to each task definition. Containers in that task receive temporary credentials scoped only to the permissions that specific service needs. Creating one dedicated role per service, and referencing that role in the matching task definition, follows the principle of least privilege because each service stays isolated from the permissions of the other five services. Keyword tip: "IAM role per task definition" is the standard secure pattern for granting AWS API access to ECS containers.
Create six separate IAM roles, each containing the required permissions for the associated ECS service, then create an IAM group and configure the ECS cluster to reference that group

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM role for an ECS task must be referenced directly by the task definition. An IAM group cannot be attached to an ECS cluster. IAM groups exist to organize IAM users, not to grant runtime permissions to ECS tasks, so there is no mechanism to connect a group to a cluster for this purpose. Keyword tip: any option that tries to bind permissions at the cluster level, instead of the task definition level, is technically invalid for ECS task authentication.
Create a new IAM instance profile containing the required permissions for the various ECS services, then associate that instance profile with the underlying EC2 instances

Explanation

Incorrect. An EC2 instance profile applies its permissions to every task running on that EC2 instance. All containers hosted on the same instance would share the same set of permissions. This breaks least privilege when multiple services with different permission needs run on shared infrastructure, and it does not scale securely as services are added or removed. Keyword tip: instance profiles grant broad, instance-wide access, which is the opposite of the fine-grained, per-service isolation this scenario requires.
Your answer is incorrect
Create a single IAM policy and use principal statements referencing the ECS tasks and assigning the required permissions, then apply the policy to the ECS service

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM policy attached directly to the ECS service controls actions on the ECS service itself, such as starting or stopping tasks. This policy does not control what a running task can do when it calls other AWS services. IAM policies also do not support principal statements that reference ECS tasks in this way. To grant a task access to other AWS services, the task definition must reference an IAM role. Keyword tip: an option that attaches permissions at the ECS service level to control task behavior is mixing up ECS management permissions with task execution permissions.

This question tests knowledge of IAM Roles for Amazon ECS Tasks. This IAM feature lets each task definition assume its own dedicated IAM role. The containers in that task receive temporary credentials scoped only to the permissions that specific task needs. Use a separate task role for each service when different services need different permissions, because an instance profile applies its permissions to every container on the instance, and an IAM group cannot attach to an ECS cluster at all. The correct scope for permissions is the task definition, not the cluster, the service, or the shared EC2 instance.

Business scenario: Everstone Technologies runs six microservices that each interact with different AWS services, such as one service that reads flood-sensor data from Amazon S3 and another that sends emergency alerts through Amazon SNS. If the team assigned one broad IAM role to the entire cluster, a compromised container in the alerting service could gain access to the data-ingestion service's permissions. By assigning a distinct IAM role to each task definition, Everstone Technologies limits the impact of a compromised container to only the permissions that specific service needs.

Question 54Incorrect

The cloud governance team at Underhill Consolidated, an agricultural technology company that manages dozens of member accounts under AWS Organizations, needs to block a short list of high-risk API actions for every IAM user and role in one specific member account, without disturbing any other permissions already granted.

What is the MOST efficient way to accomplish this?

Correct answer
Create a deny list and specify the API actions to deny

Explanation

Correct. A service control policy (SCP) configured as a deny list allows every action by default. The team only needs to name the few API actions that should be blocked. This SCP then applies to all users and roles in the member account, including the account's own administrators. Keyword tip: choose a deny list SCP whenever the scenario asks you to block a small, specific set of actions while leaving everything else allowed.
Create an allow list and specify the API actions to deny

Explanation

Incorrect. An allow list blocks every action by default. The team would need to list every single action they want to permit. This approach requires far more effort than listing only the few actions to block. Keyword tip: the term "allow list" signals that you must name every permitted action, not the denied ones.
Create an IAM policy that allows only the unrestricted API actions

Explanation

Incorrect. An IAM policy that allows only the unrestricted actions would force the team to list every single permitted API action. This list would likely be very long and hard to maintain. This IAM policy also would not restrict the root user or other account administrators, because IAM policies cannot override their permissions. Keyword tip: IAM policies alone cannot enforce restrictions on the root user or account administrators; SCPs are required for that level of control.
Your answer is incorrect
Create an IAM policy that denies the API actions for all users and roles

Explanation

Incorrect. IAM does not offer a standalone "deny policy" type that works the way this option describes. IAM policies work through explicit allow statements combined with an implicit deny for anything not listed. Even an explicit deny statement inside an IAM policy would not override the permissions of the root user or account administrators, but an SCP does. Keyword tip: when a scenario requires restrictions that apply even to privileged accounts across an entire member account, use an SCP instead of an IAM policy.

AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) control the maximum permissions available to accounts in an organization. An SCP can work as a deny list, which allows every action by default and blocks only the actions you name, or as an allow list, which blocks every action by default and permits only the actions you name. Use a deny list when you need to block a small number of specific actions and leave everything else unchanged, because you only need to list the actions to block. Unlike IAM policies, an SCP applies across the whole account and restricts access even for the root user and account administrators.

A similar situation: Underhill Consolidated might want to stop every user and role in one member account from disabling AWS CloudTrail logging or deleting the S3 buckets that store sensor data from its agricultural equipment, while still allowing all other normal operations. Applying a deny list SCP that names only those few high-risk actions blocks them across the account without requiring the team to list every other permitted action.

Question 55Correct

Riverstone Coastal, a book and media publisher, is building a new REST API on Amazon API Gateway backed by AWS Lambda functions to power its digital catalog platform. The engineering team needs to run multiple concurrent versions of this API at the same time, so the QA staff can test new catalog search features on one version while retail partners continue calling a stable production version without disruption.

What is the BEST way to provide multiple versions of the REST API?

Create an API Gateway resource policy to isolate versions and provide context to the Lambda functions

Explanation

Incorrect. An API Gateway resource policy is a JSON policy document attached to an API. A resource policy controls which principals, such as IAM users, IAM roles, or AWS accounts, can invoke the API. A resource policy can also restrict access by source IP range. A resource policy does not isolate API versions and does not pass context to backend Lambda functions. Keyword tip: a resource policy means identity-based or network-based invocation control, not versioning.
Your answer is correct
Deploy the API versions as unique stages with unique endpoints and use stage variables to provide further context

Explanation

Correct. A stage in API Gateway is a named reference to a deployment. A deployment is a snapshot of the API at one point in time. Riverstone Coastal can deploy each API version as its own stage, and each stage gets its own unique endpoint. The team can also use stage variables to configure settings for each stage separately. Stage variables are name-value pairs, similar to environment variables. The team can use a stage variable to point one stage at a testing Lambda function alias and another stage at a production Lambda function alias. This lets Riverstone Coastal run multiple API versions side by side without duplicating the API definition. Keyword tip: the terms "stages" and "stage variables" signal the standard API Gateway mechanism for managing API versions or environments.
Create an AWS Lambda authorizer to route API clients to the correct API version

Explanation

Incorrect. A Lambda authorizer is an API Gateway feature that uses a Lambda function to check whether a caller is allowed to invoke the API. The Lambda authorizer validates tokens or request parameters. The Lambda authorizer controls authentication and authorization decisions. The Lambda authorizer does not route requests to different API versions. Keyword tip: a Lambda authorizer means access control, not version management.
Deploy an HTTP proxy integration and configure the proxy with API versions

Explanation

Incorrect. An HTTP proxy integration passes a client request through to a single backend HTTP endpoint with minimal extra configuration. An HTTP proxy integration simplifies pass-through calls for one method. An HTTP proxy integration has no built-in feature for distinguishing or managing multiple API versions. Keyword tip: an HTTP proxy integration means simplified pass-through to one backend, not a versioning tool.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon API Gateway stages and stage variables as the standard way to manage multiple versions or environments of a REST API. A stage gives each API version its own unique endpoint, so different clients can call different versions independently. A stage variable lets a developer parameterize backend configuration, such as which Lambda function alias or HTTP endpoint a stage points to, without changing the underlying API definition. Resource policies control who can invoke the API, Lambda authorizers control authentication and authorization, and HTTP proxy integrations simplify pass-through routing to a single backend; none of these three features manage API versions.

Applied example: Riverstone Coastal can create a "beta" stage and a "prod" stage for its catalog search API. The "beta" stage uses a stage variable pointing to a Lambda alias running the new search logic, so QA staff can test it safely. The "prod" stage uses a stage variable pointing to the stable Lambda alias that retail partners rely on. Both stages share the same API definition, but each stage has its own endpoint and its own backend target.

Question 56Correct

Kingsford Enterprises operates a supply chain visibility platform used by regional logistics managers across multiple continents. Each week, these managers upload large volumes of shipment and inventory reporting data to a centralized Amazon S3 bucket named kingsford-reports in the us-east-1 Region.

Uploads from remote offices around the world have recently become slow. The company needs to improve data throughput and upload times with the least operational effort.

Which solution meets this requirement?

Use an AWS Managed VPN

Explanation

Incorrect. An AWS Managed VPN creates an encrypted IPsec tunnel between an on-premises network and a VPC. This VPN does not speed up data transfer to Amazon S3. AWS Managed VPN provides secure connectivity, not faster throughput. Keyword tip: when a question mentions 'VPN' in an S3 performance scenario, recognize that VPN addresses encryption and connectivity, not speed.
Your answer is correct
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the S3 bucket

Explanation

Correct. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through Amazon CloudFront edge locations near the uploading client. CloudFront then forwards the data to the S3 bucket over an optimized AWS backbone network path. This routing reduces latency and improves throughput for uploads sent from locations far from the bucket's AWS Region. Keyword tip: when a question describes global users uploading to one centralized S3 bucket with slow transfer speeds, S3 Transfer Acceleration is almost always the correct answer.
Use S3 multipart upload

Explanation

Incorrect. S3 multipart upload splits one large object into smaller parts and uploads the parts in parallel. This method improves throughput for large files. However, multipart upload still uses the same standard internet path. Multipart upload does not use edge locations, so it gives less improvement than S3 Transfer Acceleration for long-distance global uploads. Keyword tip: multipart upload optimizes large-object uploads over a single network path, while S3 Transfer Acceleration optimizes the network path itself.
Create an AWS Direct Connect connection from each remote office

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated network connection between one specific on-premises data center and a nearby AWS Region. Direct Connect does not connect many remote offices worldwide to one distant bucket's Region. Setting up a dedicated Direct Connect circuit from every global office would also be very costly and operationally complex. Keyword tip: Direct Connect solves consistent, high-bandwidth connectivity from one fixed location, not ad hoc acceleration for global uploads.

This question tests knowledge of Amazon S3 performance optimization for globally distributed upload scenarios. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration is the purpose-built feature for this use case because it uses the CloudFront global edge network to shorten the geographic distance data must travel before reaching the AWS backbone. In contrast, S3 multipart upload only splits and parallelizes chunks of a single transfer without changing the network path, and AWS Managed VPN or AWS Direct Connect solve secure or dedicated connectivity needs rather than long-distance throughput. The correct choice depends on the bottleneck: distance and latency favor Transfer Acceleration, large object size favors multipart upload, and secure or dedicated connectivity requirements favor VPN or Direct Connect.

Real-world example: A supply chain visibility startup like Kingsford Enterprises collects shipment and inventory data from regional offices on every continent, then consolidates it into one centralized Amazon S3 bucket in us-east-1 for analytics. Enabling S3 Transfer Acceleration on that bucket lets each office upload reporting data over the nearest CloudFront edge location, cutting upload times without requiring any changes to office network infrastructure. This approach scales naturally as Kingsford Enterprises adds new regional offices, since no dedicated circuits or VPN tunnels need to be provisioned for each new location.
