Question 57Incorrect

The cloud security team at Fairmount Logistics, an industrial manufacturing company with a large distributed engineering staff, has been tasked with securing several Amazon S3 buckets that are shared by a large team of users within the organization. Previously, a bucket policy was modified and the bucket inadvertently became accessible to everyone, including entities outside the organization.

Which feature or service will help the team identify similar security issues going forward with minimum effort?

Your answer is incorrect
S3 Object Lock

Explanation

Incorrect. S3 Object Lock uses a Write Once Read Many (WORM) model. This model prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a defined retention period. S3 Object Lock addresses data immutability and accidental deletion. S3 Object Lock does not address unauthorized external access caused by misconfigured policies. Keyword tip: Object Lock = WORM, retention, and legal hold, not access-policy auditing.
Access Advisor feature on the IAM console

Explanation

Incorrect. Access Advisor on the IAM console shows the last-used timestamp for an IAM role or policy. This timestamp shows when the IAM role or policy last made an AWS request. Access Advisor helps identify and remove unused IAM roles. Access Advisor does not evaluate resource-based policies on services like S3, so it cannot detect unintended external access to a bucket. Keyword tip: Access Advisor = "last accessed" data for IAM entities, not external exposure detection.
S3 Storage Class Analysis

Explanation

Incorrect. S3 Storage Class Analysis examines object access patterns over time. It uses these patterns to recommend transitions between storage classes for cost optimization. S3 Storage Class Analysis does not evaluate bucket policies and does not detect unintended public or cross-account access. Keyword tip: Storage Class Analysis = storage-tiering cost optimization, not security auditing.
Correct answer
IAM Access Analyzer

Explanation

Correct. AWS IAM Access Analyzer identifies resources in an account or organization that are shared with an entity outside a defined zone of trust. Examples of these resources include S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, and Lambda functions. IAM Access Analyzer continuously analyzes resource-based policies and generates a finding when it detects access from outside the trusted zone. This makes IAM Access Analyzer the right tool to catch unintended public or cross-account exposure with minimal ongoing effort. Keyword tip: Access Analyzer = automated detection of unintended external or cross-account resource access.

This question tests knowledge of AWS security auditing tools that detect unintended resource exposure caused by misconfigured policies. IAM Access Analyzer scans resource-based policies across an account or an organization and flags any resource, such as an S3 bucket, IAM role, or KMS key, that is accessible from outside the defined zone of trust. This makes IAM Access Analyzer the correct tool for catching accidental public or cross-account exposure with minimal manual effort. Access Advisor tracks IAM entity usage, S3 Object Lock enforces data immutability, and S3 Storage Class Analysis optimizes storage costs, and none of these three services evaluate policy-based external access risk.

Consider this scenario: Fairmount Logistics stores design blueprints and supplier contracts in S3 buckets that many engineers and external partners need to access. A single mistaken bucket policy change once exposed a bucket to the public internet. By enabling IAM Access Analyzer, the security team receives an automatic finding whenever a policy change creates unintended external access, allowing the team to correct the issue before sensitive manufacturing data is exposed.

Question 58Incorrect

A caching layer must be added in front of an Amazon RDS database to improve read performance, with the cached data encrypted and the overall solution highly available. Highmoor Alliance, a sports analytics company that processes real-time game statistics, needs to select the appropriate caching solution for this database.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode

Explanation

Correct. Amazon ElastiCache for Redis, when configured in cluster mode with replication enabled, supports encryption at rest and encryption in transit. Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode also provides high availability through automatic failover across multiple shards and read replicas. This combination meets both the encryption requirement and the high availability requirement in the scenario. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for both encryption and high availability in a cache layer, choose Redis, not Memcached.
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache built specifically to speed up read performance for DynamoDB tables. DAX cannot be placed in front of an Amazon RDS relational database. Keyword tip: DAX only works with DynamoDB, so any scenario that mentions RDS rules out DAX immediately.
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached is a simple, high-performance caching engine. Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached does not support encryption at rest or encryption in transit. Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached also does not provide built-in high availability through replication or automatic failover. Keyword tip: when a question requires encryption or automatic failover for a cache, Memcached is disqualified and Redis is the answer.
Your answer is incorrect
Amazon CloudFront with multiple origins

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network. Amazon CloudFront caches and distributes static or dynamic web content at edge locations. Amazon CloudFront does not support using an Amazon RDS database as an origin, and this scenario has only one database instance, so the idea of "multiple origins" does not apply. Keyword tip: CloudFront handles content delivery, not database query caching.

This question tests the ability to match a caching engine and configuration to specific non-functional requirements: encryption and high availability. Amazon ElastiCache offers two engines, Memcached and Redis. Only Redis, configured in cluster mode with replication, provides both encryption (at rest and in transit) and automatic failover for high availability. Memcached provides neither feature. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) and Amazon CloudFront are both caching-related services, but neither one can cache reads from an Amazon RDS relational database. The correct decision process is to first identify the type of data source (relational versus NoSQL), then match the required non-functional attributes, such as encryption and high availability, to the specific engine and mode that support them.

Consider this scenario: Highmoor Alliance runs a sports analytics platform that stores player and game statistics in Amazon RDS. During live games, read traffic spikes sharply as fans and analysts query the same statistics repeatedly. Highmoor Alliance places Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in cluster mode in front of the RDS database to absorb this repeated read traffic, encrypt the cached data, and keep the caching layer available even if one cache node fails.

Question 59Correct

A Lambda function must read transaction records from newly uploaded Amazon S3 objects and write the parsed data into an Amazon DynamoDB table for downstream settlement processing. At Cobalt Cooperative, a payment processing company that reconciles merchant transactions in near real time, this function is triggered successfully whenever a file lands in the S3 bucket, but every attempt to write the data to DynamoDB fails.

What is the probable reason for the failure?

The DynamoDB table does not have a Gateway VPC Endpoint, which is required by the Lambda function for a successful write

Explanation

Incorrect. A Gateway VPC Endpoint provides private connectivity between resources inside a VPC and Amazon S3 or DynamoDB. A Gateway VPC Endpoint is only needed when the Lambda function is configured to run inside a VPC. By default, a Lambda function does not run inside a VPC. The scenario does not describe a VPC-configured function, so no Gateway VPC Endpoint is required to reach DynamoDB over its public endpoint. Keyword tip: Gateway VPC Endpoints apply only to VPC-enabled Lambda functions, and a missing endpoint causes a network timeout, not an access-denied failure right after a successful trigger.
The Lambda function's provisioned concurrency limit has been exceeded

Explanation

Incorrect. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes execution environments for a Lambda function. Provisioned concurrency reduces cold-start latency. Exceeding provisioned concurrency affects invocation readiness and cost, not data access. Provisioned concurrency has no effect on IAM-based access control to other AWS services such as DynamoDB. Keyword tip: provisioned concurrency relates to initialization speed and latency, not to permissions.
Your answer is correct
The Lambda function does not have IAM permissions to write to DynamoDB

Explanation

Correct. A Lambda function uses an execution role. The execution role is an IAM role attached to the Lambda function. The execution role must include a policy that grants the specific DynamoDB write permission, such as dynamodb:PutItem, on the target table. Without this permission, the Lambda function triggers and runs, but the DynamoDB write call fails with an access-denied error, which matches the failure described in the scenario. Keyword tip: when a Lambda function triggers correctly but fails only on a specific downstream API call, suspect a missing IAM execution role permission for that action.
The Lambda function's reserved concurrency limit has been exceeded

Explanation

Incorrect. Reserved concurrency reserves a fixed number of concurrent execution environments for a Lambda function. Reaching the reserved concurrency limit causes invocation throttling. Throttling does not cause a permission-related write failure to DynamoDB. In this scenario, the Lambda function already triggers and runs successfully, so concurrency is not the cause. Keyword tip: reserved concurrency problems show up as throttling errors, such as HTTP 429 or TooManyRequestsException, not as write failures to a downstream data store.

This question tests understanding of AWS Lambda execution roles and IAM permission scoping when a Lambda function must interact with another AWS service, such as Amazon DynamoDB. The execution role attached to a Lambda function must explicitly include the required actions, such as dynamodb:PutItem or dynamodb:UpdateItem, on the target resource. Permissions are never inherited automatically just because the Lambda function triggers successfully from an event source like Amazon S3. When troubleshooting a failure like this, first isolate whether the failure happens at invocation, which points to concurrency or event configuration issues, or at a specific downstream API call, which points to IAM permission issues; these two failure types have very different root causes and fixes. Networking constructs like Gateway VPC Endpoints are only relevant if the Lambda function is explicitly configured to run inside a VPC, which is not the default behavior.

Real-world example: Cobalt Cooperative runs a Lambda function that parses merchant settlement files from Amazon S3 and writes transaction records to a DynamoDB table for reconciliation. The Lambda function's event trigger from S3 works correctly, confirming that the function itself invokes without issue. When the DynamoDB write step fails, the Cobalt Cooperative engineering team checks the Lambda execution role first, because a successful trigger combined with a failed downstream write is a strong signal of a missing IAM permission rather than a concurrency or networking problem.

Question 60Incorrect

Hallmark Industries, a satellite communications provider headquartered in Denver, runs a serverless application on AWS that processes telemetry data from its ground stations. The application is built using AWS SAM, and the current process requires a full CloudFormation deployment for every code change before a developer can test it.

The development team now wants an accelerated workflow that lets a developer push incremental code changes for testing without redeploying the entire application on every commit, while also minimizing deployment time.

What should the developer do to meet these requirements?

Correct answer
Use the sam sync command from the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) to deploy incremental changes

Explanation

Correct. The sam sync command is designed for fast, iterative development of AWS SAM applications. The sam sync command detects local code and infrastructure changes and updates only the changed resources directly, using direct API calls when possible instead of a full AWS CloudFormation update. This direct-update approach makes the sam sync command much faster than a full deployment, which matches the requirement to minimize deployment time. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for fast iterative testing and minimal deployment time in an AWS SAM application, the sam sync command is the correct tool.
Use the cdk deploy command from the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy incremental changes to AWS for testing

Explanation

Incorrect. The cdk deploy command deploys an entire AWS CDK stack, or the changed resources within that stack, through a standard AWS CloudFormation update. The cdk deploy command is a general-purpose deployment mechanism for AWS CDK projects, not a fast, incremental testing tool for AWS SAM applications. This scenario is built around AWS SAM, so the cdk deploy command does not apply. Keyword tip: the cdk deploy command is the AWS CDK equivalent of a full stack deployment, similar in scope to the sam deploy command, not a fast-sync mechanism.
Your answer is incorrect
Use the sam deploy command from the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) to deploy incremental changes

Explanation

Incorrect. The sam deploy command performs a full deployment through AWS CloudFormation. The sam deploy command packages the application and deploys it, or its changed resources, using a complete change-set-based update, even for small code edits. This process is reliable for production releases, but the sam deploy command does not minimize deployment time during active local testing, because the sam deploy command lacks the direct-update optimizations built into the sam sync command. Keyword tip: the sam deploy command is the standard, AWS CloudFormation-backed production deployment path, while the sam sync command is the fast local development iteration path.
Use the cdk diff command from the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) to deploy incremental changes to AWS for testing

Explanation

Incorrect. The cdk diff command does not deploy anything. The cdk diff command only compares the local AWS CDK code against the currently deployed AWS CloudFormation stack and shows the differences. Because the cdk diff command never pushes changes to AWS, the cdk diff command cannot meet a requirement to deploy incremental changes for testing. Keyword tip: the word "diff" in a command name signals a read-only comparison action, not a deployment action.

This question tests knowledge of the AWS SAM CLI commands used during the serverless application development lifecycle. The sam sync command is built for rapid iterative development. The sam sync command detects local changes and pushes only those changes directly to the deployed resources, which skips the overhead of a full AWS CloudFormation change set. The sam deploy command and the cdk deploy command both perform complete, auditable stack deployments through AWS CloudFormation, which makes them suitable for staging or production releases but too slow for constant local testing. The cdk diff command only previews differences and never deploys anything. The key decision signal is the combination of "incremental changes" and "minimizing deployment time," which points directly to a synchronization command rather than a full stack deployment or a comparison-only command.

Practical example: Hallmark Industries has a developer who is testing a bug fix in a Lambda function that processes satellite telemetry alerts. The developer runs the sam sync command to push only the changed function code to the deployed AWS SAM application in seconds, tests the fix immediately, and repeats this cycle multiple times before running a full sam deploy command once the fix is confirmed and ready for the staging environment.

Question 61Incorrect

The platform engineering team at Brackenridge Logistics, a transportation logistics provider that manages bus routing and attendance tracking for a K-12 school district, runs its application on a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances behind an Auto Scaling group. The application stores route and attendance data in an Amazon DynamoDB table, and every instance can write updates to the table.

The team has noticed that some instances occasionally read outdated attendance records immediately after another instance writes an update. The team must modify the application so that every query returns the latest committed data.

Which change should the team make?

Your answer is incorrect
Cache the database writes using Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX).

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB. DAX improves read latency for read-heavy workloads. DAX does not guarantee that a read returns the most recent write, because cached data can also become stale. DAX solves a performance problem, not a consistency problem. Keyword tip: DAX is about read speed, not read freshness.
Correct answer
Set the ConsistentRead parameter to true when calling GetItem.

Explanation

Correct. DynamoDB uses eventually consistent reads by default. An eventually consistent read can return stale data for a short time after a write. Setting the ConsistentRead parameter to true on GetItem, Query, or Scan forces DynamoDB to perform a strongly consistent read. A strongly consistent read always returns the most recent successful write. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes stale reads right after writes, choose ConsistentRead=true.
Use the UpdateGlobalTable API to create a global secondary index.

Explanation

Incorrect. There is no UpdateGlobalTable API operation for creating a global secondary index. Global secondary indexes are created through the UpdateTable API operation. Even a correctly created global secondary index only supports eventually consistent reads. A global secondary index cannot fix a stale-read problem on the base table. Keyword tip: global secondary indexes never support strongly consistent reads.
Use the TransactWriteItems API when issuing PutItem actions.

Explanation

Incorrect. TransactWriteItems groups multiple write operations into one all-or-nothing transaction. This feature guarantees write atomicity across items. This feature does not change how a later read operation retrieves data. The team needs a read-side setting, not a write-side transaction feature. Keyword tip: TransactWriteItems solves atomic writes, not stale reads.

DynamoDB supports two read consistency models: eventually consistent reads, which are the default and may not reflect a very recent write, and strongly consistent reads, which always return the latest successful write. A developer enables strongly consistent reads by setting the ConsistentRead parameter to true on GetItem, Query, or Scan, at the cost of higher read capacity usage and slightly higher latency. Choose eventually consistent reads when the application can tolerate brief staleness and needs maximum throughput at lower cost. Choose strongly consistent reads when the application logic depends on always seeing the most recent write, such as reading data right after writing it. TransactWriteItems, DAX, and global secondary indexes each address a different concern (write atomicity, cache-based read speed, and alternate query patterns) and none of them guarantee that a read reflects the latest write.

Use case: A school district transportation system like Brackenridge Logistics tracks bus attendance in near real time, and a dispatcher may write an attendance update on one EC2 instance while a parent-facing status page on another instance immediately queries the same record. Setting ConsistentRead to true for that query ensures the status page always shows the latest attendance update instead of a stale value from a moment earlier. This pattern is common whenever an application performs a write and then immediately needs to read back the same data to confirm the update took effect.

References:

Question 62Incorrect

Ironwood Institute, a food and beverage producer, operates a real-time analytics pipeline that ingests sensor data from packaging lines through an Amazon Kinesis data stream. A developer at Ironwood Institute has built an AWS Lambda function named IronwoodStreamProcessor to process these records, and load testing shows the function will be invoked 40 times per second, with each invocation taking approximately 80 seconds to complete.

What must the developer do to guarantee the function processes this Kinesis stream without throttling errors?

Your answer is incorrect
Implement exponential backoff in the function code

Explanation

Incorrect. Exponential backoff is a retry strategy. Exponential backoff spaces out repeated calls after a throttling error. This strategy helps a client handle temporary throttling. This strategy does not fix a structural capacity problem. In this scenario, the required concurrency permanently exceeds the account's available concurrency. The developer must raise the account's concurrency limit instead of slowing down retries. Keyword tip: exponential backoff fixes temporary throttling, not a sustained capacity shortfall that needs a limit increase.
Increase the reserved concurrency limit for the function

Explanation

Incorrect. Reserved concurrency sets aside a dedicated pool of concurrency for one function. This dedicated pool comes from the account's total Regional concurrency limit. AWS always keeps a minimum unreserved pool of 100 concurrent executions available for other functions. With a default account limit of 1,000, the developer could reserve at most 900 units for this function, which is still far below the required 3,200. Keyword tip: reserved concurrency reallocates existing capacity; reserved concurrency cannot create new capacity beyond the account's Regional limit.
No action is required, as AWS Lambda can easily accommodate this requirement

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Lambda scales automatically to run many requests at the same time. However, all functions in a Region share one default account-level concurrency limit of 1,000 concurrent executions. The developer must calculate the required concurrency as the invocation rate multiplied by the average duration. For this function, 40 invocations per second multiplied by 80 seconds equals 3,200 concurrent executions, which is higher than the default limit. Keyword tip: always calculate concurrency as (invocations per second) multiplied by (average duration in seconds), then compare the result to the account limit.
Correct answer
Contact AWS and request an increase to the account's concurrent execution limit

Explanation

Correct. The calculated concurrency requirement for this function is 3,200 concurrent executions. This requirement is higher than the default Regional concurrency limit of 1,000. The only way to let the function run at this scale without throttling errors is to submit a service limit increase request to AWS Support. Keyword tip: when calculated concurrency is higher than the default account-level limit, the required action is a support-requested limit increase.

AWS Lambda concurrency is calculated as the invocation rate multiplied by the average execution duration. Each AWS account has a default Regional concurrency limit of 1,000 concurrent executions, and this limit is shared across all functions in that Region. Reserved concurrency lets a developer dedicate part of this shared pool to one function, but AWS always keeps a minimum unreserved pool of 100 concurrent executions for other functions, so reserved concurrency cannot exceed the account limit. When a function's calculated concurrency requirement is higher than the account's total limit, the only correct action is to request a service limit increase from AWS Support; exponential backoff only helps with temporary throttling errors and does not solve a sustained capacity shortfall.

Consider this scenario: Ironwood Institute processes packaging-line sensor data from many production facilities through a single Kinesis stream, and its analytics team calculates that peak processing load will need thousands of concurrent Lambda executions. This requirement is far above the AWS default concurrency limit, so the development team must submit a limit increase request before the peak production season starts. Submitting the request early ensures the pipeline does not throttle during high-volume periods.

Question 63Incorrect

Beacon Corporation runs its video conferencing platform as a set of microservices deployed in Docker containers on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS). A developer on the platform team is investigating call-quality complaints and needs to capture trace information showing how requests flow between the microservices to pinpoint where latency is introduced.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

Install the AWS X-Ray daemon locally on a separate Amazon EC2 instance and instrument Beacon Corporation's Amazon ECS microservices using the X-Ray SDK.

Explanation

Incorrect. Running the X-Ray daemon on a separate, standalone EC2 instance does not give the Amazon ECS tasks a reliable local path to send trace data. This separate instance does not scale or fail over together with Beacon Corporation's containerized microservices. Keyword tip: the X-Ray daemon must run in the same network namespace or be reachable through task networking with the instrumented application, not on an unrelated instance.
Correct answer
Create a Docker image that runs the AWS X-Ray daemon, upload it to a Docker image repository, and deploy it to Beacon Corporation's Amazon ECS cluster.

Explanation

Correct. The AWS X-Ray daemon must run as a container next to the instrumented microservices. Beacon Corporation can package the X-Ray daemon in its own Docker image and deploy it into the same Amazon ECS cluster, either as a sidecar container in the task definition or as a separate service on the same network. This setup lets the microservices send trace segments to the daemon over localhost or the local network. This is the AWS-recommended pattern for tracing containerized workloads on Amazon ECS. Keyword tip: when a question mentions Docker containers on Amazon ECS plus distributed tracing, look for the option that packages the X-Ray daemon as its own container image deployed alongside the application.
Your answer is incorrect
Install the AWS X-Ray daemon on each of the Amazon ECS container instances in Beacon Corporation's cluster.

Explanation

Incorrect. This option installs the X-Ray daemon directly on the Amazon ECS container instances, which are the underlying EC2 hosts. This approach bypasses the containerized deployment model. This approach is not supported for Fargate launch type tasks, because Fargate does not give Beacon Corporation access to the underlying host. Keyword tip: any option that installs software on the ECS host operating system instead of inside a task or container is a warning sign in containerized tracing scenarios.
Install the Amazon CloudWatch agent on the container image and use the CloudWatch SDK to publish custom metrics from each of Beacon Corporation's microservices.

Explanation

Incorrect. The Amazon CloudWatch agent and CloudWatch custom metrics capture numeric monitoring data, such as counts and aggregated latency values. CloudWatch does not capture distributed trace segments that show the call path and timing across microservices. Beacon Corporation needs trace data to see how a single request moves between microservices, which CloudWatch metrics cannot provide. Keyword tip: CloudWatch is for metrics and logs, while AWS X-Ray is the service built specifically for distributed tracing between services.

This question tests knowledge of how to deploy the AWS X-Ray daemon in a containerized environment to enable distributed tracing across microservices. The X-Ray daemon must run close to the instrumented application, typically as a sidecar container in the same Amazon ECS task definition, using port mappings and the correct network mode. This setup lets trace segments emitted by the AWS X-Ray SDK reach the AWS X-Ray service without depending on the underlying compute host. Amazon CloudWatch, in contrast, is designed for metrics and logs, not end-to-end trace data, and installing the daemon on the host operating system or an unrelated EC2 instance breaks the expected communication path.

In practice: Beacon Corporation's video conferencing platform depends on fast communication between microservices such as call setup, media routing, and recording. When users report choppy calls, the developer team packages the X-Ray daemon as its own container and deploys it alongside each microservice task on Amazon ECS. This configuration lets them trace a single call request across every microservice hop and quickly identify which service adds the most latency.

Question 64Correct

A recent internal security audit at a regional airline found that database credentials for a production application had gone unrotated for several months, in direct violation of company policy. The application, built by Nightingale Trust and headquartered in Denver, runs on AWS Lambda and connects to a PostgreSQL database hosted on Amazon RDS.

In response to the audit, the security team now mandates that database credentials be rotated every week.

What strategy should the developer adopt to manage the database credentials for the application?

Enable IAM database authentication and manage weekly rotation manually.

Explanation

Incorrect. IAM database authentication lets an IAM user or role generate a short-lived authentication token to connect to Amazon RDS. This token replaces the need to store a password. IAM database authentication does not include a built-in schedule for rotating credentials every week. The developer would still need to build and manage that rotation process manually. Keyword tip: IAM database authentication removes the need to store a password, but it does not provide automatic rotation on a schedule.
Your answer is correct
Deploy AWS Secrets Manager to store database credentials and set up automatic weekly rotation.

Explanation

Correct. AWS Secrets Manager stores database credentials securely and supports automatic rotation on a defined schedule, including weekly rotation. AWS Secrets Manager uses a built-in Lambda rotation function for Amazon RDS, so the rotation happens without manual steps. This directly matches the requirement for automated weekly credential rotation. Keyword tip: when a scenario asks for automatic credential rotation on a fixed schedule, AWS Secrets Manager is the expected answer.
Store database credentials in Amazon S3 buckets with versioning enabled, rotating, and uploading new credentials weekly.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Amazon S3 has no built-in feature for rotating secrets. Storing credentials as objects in Amazon S3 and rotating them by hand each week is a manual process, and it also leaves the credentials stored as plain, unmanaged data. This approach does not meet the requirement for automated rotation. Keyword tip: S3 versioning tracks changes to stored objects, but versioning is not a secrets management or rotation feature.
Store the credentials in environment variables of the Lambda function and manually update them every week.

Explanation

Incorrect. Storing credentials in Lambda environment variables means anyone with read access to the function configuration can see those credentials. This approach also requires the developer to manually update the environment variables and redeploy the function every week. This manual process is labor-intensive and increases security risk if the environment variables are not tightly access-controlled. Keyword tip: plain Lambda environment variables used for secrets storage is a common distractor pattern that signals poor secrets hygiene.

This question tests knowledge of secrets management for applications that require periodic, automated credential rotation. AWS Secrets Manager is built for this exact use case: it stores secrets securely, integrates directly with Amazon RDS, and triggers a rotation Lambda function on a schedule the developer defines, with no manual steps required. IAM database authentication solves a different problem — it removes the need to store a password at all, but it does not provide scheduled rotation. Amazon S3 storage and Lambda environment variables both lack any native, secure rotation capability, so both require manual work and carry higher security risk when a strict rotation policy is mandated. The decision rule is simple: when a scenario requires automated, scheduled credential rotation, AWS Secrets Manager is the correct choice over manual or ad hoc alternatives.

Applied example: Nightingale Trust operates a flight-scheduling application that queries a PostgreSQL database on Amazon RDS from an AWS Lambda function. After the security audit exposed months of unrotated credentials, the development team configures AWS Secrets Manager to store the database credentials and rotate them automatically every week using the built-in RDS rotation Lambda function. This removes the manual rotation burden from the team and closes the audit finding without any code changes to how the Lambda function retrieves the credentials at runtime.

Question 65Incorrect

A serverless solution is needed to support phased releases of static websites currently hosted across several different version control systems, with each deployment automatically triggered by a Git branch merge and all traffic served over HTTPS. Granite Authority, a fast-growing music streaming platform based in Austin, Texas, needs this capability to roll out updates to its promotional landing pages quickly and without managing infrastructure.

Which option offers the LOWEST operational overhead?

Your answer is incorrect
Use Amazon S3 to host the websites, and create a manual script to deploy changes when there are code merges in the version control systems.

Explanation

Incorrect. Amazon S3 can host static websites at low cost, but this option requires a custom deployment script to detect code merges and trigger updates. Building and maintaining that script adds manual effort and ongoing maintenance work. Keyword tip: any option that requires a custom or manual script for deployment automation signals higher operational overhead than a fully managed CI/CD-integrated service.
Use AWS Elastic Beanstalk for hosting and use AWS CodeStar to manage deployments and workflows.

Explanation

Incorrect. AWS Elastic Beanstalk is built for dynamic, multi-tier applications. Elastic Beanstalk still requires provisioning and managing underlying compute resources, such as EC2 instances, load balancers, and auto scaling groups. Adding AWS CodeStar on top of Elastic Beanstalk adds another layer of configuration. This configuration is not needed for hosting simple static websites. Keyword tip: Elastic Beanstalk signals managed infrastructure, not a fully serverless, zero-infrastructure static hosting solution.
Correct answer
Use AWS Amplify for hosting, connect corresponding repository branches, and initiate deployments by merging changes to the needed branch.

Explanation

Correct. AWS Amplify is a fully managed, serverless hosting service built specifically for static websites. AWS Amplify connects directly to a Git repository and automatically triggers a build and deployment whenever code is merged into a connected branch. AWS Amplify serves content over HTTPS by default and supports separate branch-based environments, which enables phased releases. This setup requires no server management and no custom deployment scripts. Keyword tip: when a scenario describes static site hosting with Git-based continuous deployment and minimal operational overhead, AWS Amplify is almost always the correct choice.
Deploy websites on separate Amazon EC2 instances for each environment, use AWS CodeDeploy for automation, and link it with the version control systems.

Explanation

Incorrect. Hosting websites on Amazon EC2 instances is not a serverless approach. This option requires provisioning, patching, and running instances continuously for each environment, in addition to configuring AWS CodeDeploy and connecting it to the version control systems. These extra steps significantly increase operational overhead compared to a serverless static hosting service. Keyword tip: EC2-based hosting always implies infrastructure management, which conflicts with a stated 'serverless' requirement.

This question tests the ability to match a serverless, Git-triggered static hosting requirement to the correct AWS service. AWS Amplify is purpose-built for this exact pattern: it connects to a Git repository, automatically deploys on branch merges, serves content over HTTPS by default, and supports separate branches as separate environments for phased releases, all without server management. Elastic Beanstalk and EC2-based approaches fail the serverless requirement because both require provisioning and managing compute resources. The Amazon S3 option fails the low-overhead requirement because it depends on a custom script that the team must build and maintain. When a scenario combines static content, Git branch merges as the deployment trigger, HTTPS delivery, and a demand for minimal operational overhead, AWS Amplify is the correct answer.

Use case: Granite Authority could connect its marketing repository to AWS Amplify, mapping each Git branch to a separate environment, such as a staging branch for internal review and a main branch for production. When a developer merges a new artist promotion page into the main branch, AWS Amplify automatically builds and deploys the update to the live site over HTTPS, with no manual server configuration or custom scripting required.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amplify/latest/userguide/welcome.html
